translate.tr: Every lecture has a practical class.
wrong: Not every lecture has a practical class.
Every practical class has two lectures.

translate.tr: He has to register for the exam.
wrong: He has to pass the exam.
She has to register for the exam.
He doesn't have to register for the exam.

translate.tr: The lecture hall is completely full today.
wrong: The lecture hall is completely empty today.
The lecture hall was completely full yesterday.
The library is completely full today.

informatik-a21-10-studium:1.text:
In December studying gets hard for Viktor. There's an assignment due every week, usually on Sunday at midnight. Viktor takes notes in every lecture, but there are still some problems he doesn't understand.

So he starts a study group with three fellow students. They meet in the library every Wednesday. On Friday they go to the tutorial together, because the tutor explains everything very well. But there's one question she can't answer, so Viktor goes to the professor's office hours.

Viktor is afraid he'll fail the exam. But the work paid off: in February he gets a good grade, a 2. In Austria that means “good”.
questions: When is the assignment usually due?
Where does the study group meet?
Why does Viktor go to the professor's office hours?
What grade does Viktor get?

translate.tr: There's an assignment due every week.
wrong: There's an assignment due every month.
There's no assignment due this week.

translate.tr: Viktor starts a study group with fellow students.
wrong: Viktor is looking for a study group with fellow students.
Viktor started a study group with fellow students.
Viktor starts a project with fellow students.

mathe-a2-uni:0.text:
On Monday Elif sits in the lecture “Analysis 1” for the first time. The lecture hall is full, and the professor starts right away. First he writes a definition on the board: the set of natural numbers. Then he shows a function with one variable.

After that he proves a theorem. The proof is only half a page long, but Elif doesn't understand it. She thinks: “At school we only solved equations. Here we have to prove everything!”

After the lecture she talks to her fellow student Tobias. He says that everyone feels like that at the beginning. “If you read the proof again slowly at home, you'll definitely understand it.” In the evening Elif reads her notes and finally understands the proof. She is very proud of herself.

gloss.mal: time (zum ersten Mal — for the first time)
gloss.halbe: half (eine halbe Seite — half a page)
gloss.geht: (es geht allen so) everyone feels like that
gloss.stolz: proud (stolz auf sich — proud of herself)

questions: What does the professor write on the board first?
What did Elif do at school?
What does Tobias say?
When does Elif understand the proof?

translate.tr: The proof is only half a page long.
wrong: The proof is a whole page long.
The definition is only half a page long.

translate.tr: The set of natural numbers is infinite.
wrong: The set of natural numbers is finite.
The set of even numbers is infinite.

mathe-a2-uni:1.text:
Every Thursday Elif has an exercise class. There she sometimes has to work through a problem on the board. This week she got five problems, and she's solving them with Tobias in the library.

In the first problem they have to reduce a fraction. That's easy. The second problem is about a root: is the square root of two a fraction? Tobias doesn't know. Elif reads the definition in the lecture notes again carefully. Then she says: “Suppose the square root of two is a fraction. That leads to a contradiction. So it isn't a fraction!”

On Thursday Elif works through exactly this problem on the board. The tutor is pleased. Afterwards she goes to the lecture with Tobias, because today they don't want to be late.

gloss.vorrechnen: to work through (a problem) on the board
gloss.geht: goes; es geht um … — it's about …
gloss.spät: late (zu spät kommen — to be late)

questions: What does Elif sometimes have to do in the exercise class?
Who does Elif solve the problems with?
What does Elif read again in the lecture notes?
What does Elif show in the second problem?

translate.tr: Every Thursday Elif has an exercise class.
wrong: Every Thursday Elif has a lecture.
Every Friday Elif has an exercise class.
This Thursday Elif has an exercise class.

translate.tr: We have to reduce a fraction.
wrong: We have to take a root.
We don't have to reduce a fraction.
They have to reduce a fraction.
That doesn't lead to a contradiction.

mathe-a21-02-prozentrechnung:0.text:
In January there are end-of-season sales. Sophie sees a jacket in a shop window. It used to cost 80 euros; now it's reduced by 30 per cent. The old price is the base value, 30 per cent is the percentage.

Sophie uses the rule of three: 100 per cent is 80 euros, so 1 per cent is 80 cents. 30 per cent is then 24 euros. That's the percentage value. So the jacket only costs 56 euros now.

At the checkout Sophie shows her student card and gets another 10 per cent off. The receipt also shows the VAT: 20 per cent is already included in the price. Sophie is glad, because from February the shop raises its prices again.
questions: By how many per cent is the jacket reduced?
How much does the jacket cost after the discount in the window?
What does Sophie show at the checkout?

translate.tr: The jacket is reduced by thirty per cent.
wrong: The jacket has gone up by thirty per cent.
The jacket is reduced by thirteen per cent.

translate.tr: The old price is the base value.
wrong: The new price is the base value.
The old price is the percentage value.

translate.tr: In February the shop raises its prices.
wrong: In February the shop lowers its prices.
In January the shop raises its prices.

mathe-a21-02-prozentrechnung:1.text:
For his birthday Paul got 1000 euros from his grandma. He doesn't want to spend the money but to invest it. He goes to the bank with his father.

The adviser explains: “On the savings account the interest rate is two per cent. You get the interest annually.” Paul calculates: after a year the balance is 1020 euros. So the increase is only twenty euros.

Then Paul asks: “And if I borrow money?” The adviser laughs: “For a loan you pay more interest, for example six per cent.” Paul understands: the bank earns money on the difference. In the end he invests the money for three years. After that it's a bit more than 1061 euros.
questions: How high is the interest rate on the savings account?
How much is the balance after a year?
What does the bank earn its money on?

translate.tr: Paul invests the money for three years.
wrong: Paul spends the money over three years.
Paul invests the money for thirty years.

translate.tr: For a loan you pay more interest.
wrong: For a loan you get more interest.
For a loan you pay less interest.

mathe-a21-03-lineare-funktionen:0.text:
In the maths lesson Ms Berger draws a coordinate system on the board. It has two axes: the x-axis and the y-axis. The point in the middle is called the origin.

Then she writes down the function y = 2x + 1. “This is a linear function. Its graph is always a straight line.” The class makes a table of values. For x = 0, y = 1; for x = 1, y = 3; for x = 2, y = 5.

Ms Berger asks: “What is the slope?” Jakob puts his hand up: “Two. When x gets bigger by one, y gets bigger by two.” The line doesn't go through the origin, because it crosses the y-axis at 1.

gloss.um: by (um eins größer — bigger by one)

questions: What is the point in the middle called?
What is y for x = 2?
Why doesn't the line go through the origin?

translate.tr: The graph is always a straight line.
wrong: The graph is always a curve.
The graph is never a straight line.

translate.tr: The class makes a table of values.
wrong: The class draws a coordinate system.
The teacher makes a table of values.

mathe-a21-03-lineare-funktionen:1.text:
Elena needs a new phone plan. There are two offers. Plan A has a basic fee of ten euros a month, and each minute costs five cents. Plan B has no basic fee, but each minute costs fifteen cents.

Elena makes a table of values for both plans and draws the graphs. For both, the price depends on the minutes. Each function assigns a price to the number of minutes. The line of plan B goes through the origin and is steeper. With plan B the price is proportional to the minutes.

The point of intersection is at a hundred minutes. There both plans cost fifteen euros. Elena phones a lot, more than a hundred minutes. So for her plan A is cheaper.
questions: Which plan has no basic fee?
Where is the point of intersection?
Which plan is cheaper for Elena?

translate.tr: The price depends on the minutes.
wrong: The price doesn't depend on the minutes.
The minutes depend on the price.

translate.tr: The line of plan B is steeper.
wrong: The line of plan B is flatter.
The line of plan A is steeper.

translate.tr: Plan A has a basic fee of ten euros.
wrong: Plan A has a basic fee of fifteen euros.
Plan A has no basic fee.

mathe-a21-04-potenzen:0.text:
Ms Berger writes “zwei hoch drei” on the board. “This is a power. The two is the base, the three is the exponent. The exponent tells you how many times to multiply the base by itself: two times two times two is eight.”

If the exponent is two, you square the number. That's how the square numbers come about: one, four, nine, sixteen. With powers of ten you can write big numbers briefly. Ten to the power of six is a million.

Then it gets harder. Minus two to the power of two is positive, namely four. But minus two to the power of three is negative, namely minus eight. Jakob is amazed: “The exponent decides the sign!”

gloss.hoch: to the power of (zwei hoch drei — two to the power of three)

questions: In “zwei hoch drei”, what is the base?
Which number is ten to the power of six?
What is minus two to the power of three?

mathe-a21-04-potenzen:1.text:
In the biology lesson Mr Wimmer shows a video from a lab. A bacterium divides every twenty minutes. One bacterium becomes two, then four, then eight. The number keeps doubling.

Lea calculates: after one hour there are eight bacteria, after three hours already 512, that is two to the power of nine. The growth isn't linear but exponential. At first the number grows slowly, then it rises rapidly.

Mr Wimmer asks: “And after 24 hours?” That's two to the power of 72. The number is so big that you can only write it with a power of ten. It's of the order of ten to the power of 21. In such a short period of time! Luckily bacteria in nature don't always have enough food.

gloss.alle: every (alle zwanzig Minuten — every twenty minutes)
gloss.hoch: to the power of (zwei hoch neun — two to the power of nine)

questions: How often does a bacterium divide?
How many bacteria are there after three hours?
What kind of growth is this?

translate.tr: At first the number grows slowly.
wrong: At the end the number grows slowly.
At first the number grows rapidly.

mathe-a21-05-wahrscheinlichkeit:0.text:
On Sunday Lena and Tom play a dice game. At the start you need a six, otherwise you can't begin. Tom rolls three times and doesn't get a six. He's annoyed.

Lena explains: “When you roll the dice, chance decides. Every number from one to six is equally likely. So the probability of a six is one sixth.”

Tom asks: “And how likely is a seven?” Lena laughs: “That's impossible, the probability is zero. But it's certain that you'll roll a number less than seven.” On the fourth try Tom finally rolls a six. The game will probably go on for another hour now.

gloss.mal: time (beim vierten Mal — on the fourth try)

questions: Why is Tom annoyed?
What is the probability of a six?
What is impossible?

translate.tr: When you roll the dice, chance decides.
wrong: When you roll the dice, strategy decides.
When you play chess, chance decides.
A six is more likely than the other numbers.

mathe-a21-05-wahrscheinlichkeit:1.text:
At the school party there's a raffle. In the box there are 200 tickets: 50 winners and 150 blanks. So the chance of winning for one ticket is 50 out of 200, that's 25 per cent.

Max draws three tickets. The first is a blank, and so is the second. On the third try he's lucky: a winner! He wins a cinema voucher.

Next to it there's a wheel of fortune with eight equal sections. Only one section is the main prize. The probability of this event is one eighth. Sara spins the wheel. By chance it stops on the main prize! Everyone cheers. Max says: “That's not talent, that's pure chance.”
questions: How many winning tickets are in the box?
What does Max win?
What is the probability of the main prize?

translate.tr: The chance of winning is twenty-five per cent.
wrong: The chance of winning is fifty per cent.
The chance of losing is twenty-five per cent.

translate.tr: The first ticket is a blank.
wrong: The first ticket is a winner.
The last ticket is a blank.

mathe-a21-06-statistik:0.text:
The school newspaper wants to know: how long do the teenagers at our school sleep? The school has 600 students. Asking all of them is too much work. So Mia and Jonas take a sample: they survey 60 people.

At first they only want to ask their own class. But Ms Berger says: “That's not representative. Younger children sleep longer.” So they choose six people from each class.

Each person gets a short questionnaire. At the weekend Mia and Jonas analyse the questionnaires. The answer “seven hours” has the highest frequency: 24 out of 60, so 40 per cent. They show the result in a pie chart.
questions: How many people do Mia and Jonas survey?
Why don't they survey only their own class?
Which answer has the highest frequency?

translate.tr: At the weekend they analyse the questionnaires.
wrong: At the weekend they hand out the questionnaires.
On Monday they analyse the questionnaires.

mathe-a21-06-statistik:1.text:
There are seven children in Jonas's study group. They compare their pocket money per month. The data set is: 15, 20, 10, 25, 15, 20 and 200 euros. Felix gets the 200 euros. His parents are very rich.

Jonas works out the mean: the sum is 305 euros, divided by seven that's about 44 euros. “We get 44 euros on average? That's not true!” says Lisa. Felix is an outlier, and an outlier distorts the mean.

Then they sort the values: 10, 15, 15, 20, 20, 25, 200. The value in the middle is 20. That's the median. The range is 200 minus 10, so 190 euros. For this group the median is much more meaningful than the mean.

gloss.stimmt: is right (das stimmt nicht — that's not true)

questions: Who gets 200 euros?
What is the median?
What distorts the mean?

wrong: An outlier doesn't affect the mean.
First they add up the values.
At the end they sort the values.

translate.tr: Here the median is more meaningful.
wrong: Here the mean is more meaningful.
Here the median is less meaningful.

mathe-a21-07-koerper:0.text:
Lukas is getting an aquarium for his fish. It's shaped like a cuboid: 60 centimetres long, 30 centimetres wide and 40 centimetres high. How much water does he need?

His father explains: “First you work out the base area: 60 times 30, that's 1800 square centimetres. The volume is base area times height, so 1800 times 40.” That makes 72,000 cubic centimetres. A litre has 1000 cubic centimetres, so it's 72 litres.

Then Lukas wants to know how much glass you need for the aquarium. It's open at the top. He draws the net and adds up the areas: the surface area without a lid is 9000 square centimetres. In the evening they fill the aquarium with water.
questions: What shape is the aquarium?
How much water fits in the aquarium?
What does Lukas draw for the surface area?

translate.tr: The volume is base area times height.
wrong: The volume is base area plus height.
The area is base times height.

translate.tr: A litre has a thousand cubic centimetres.
wrong: A litre has a hundred cubic centimetres.
A kilogram has a thousand cubic centimetres.

translate.tr: They fill the aquarium with water.
wrong: They pour the water out of the aquarium.
They wash the aquarium with water.

mathe-a21-07-koerper:1.text:
In the supermarket Lena is holding a tin of tomatoes. The tin is a cylinder. Its diameter is eight centimetres, so the radius is four centimetres. The height is ten centimetres.

At home Lena looks up the formula: volume equals pi times radius squared times height. Pi is about 3.14. She calculates: 3.14 times 16 times 10, that's about 502 cubic centimetres. So the tin holds roughly half a litre.

Afterwards Lena eats an ice cream. The cone is a cone. A cone has only a third of the volume of a cylinder with the same base and height. The same rule applies to a pyramid. Lena thinks: “That's why there's always so little ice cream in the cone!”

gloss.halben: half (einen halben Liter — half a litre)

questions: What is the radius of the tin?
About how much does the tin hold?
What is the ice cream cone?

translate.tr: The same rule applies to a pyramid.
wrong: A different rule applies to a pyramid.
The same rule applies to a cylinder.

mathe-a21-08-matura:0.text:
Today Sophie is taking the written Matura in mathematics. The exam takes 270 minutes. On the table are the calculator and the official formula booklet. You're allowed to use both.

The first part has lots of short tasks. It's about basic competences: equations, functions, percentages. Sophie is well prepared and works quickly. The second part is harder. The tasks are longer, and Sophie comes under time pressure. She takes a deep breath and concentrates on the next task.

Two weeks later the result comes. According to the grading scale you need at least 36 points for a “good”. Sophie has 38 points. She has passed the Matura! In the autumn she can study at TU Wien.

gloss.später: later (zwei Wochen später — two weeks later)

questions: How long does the exam take?
What is Sophie allowed to use?
How many points does Sophie have?

translate.tr: You're allowed to use the formula booklet.
wrong: You're not allowed to use the formula booklet.
You're not allowed to use the calculator.
Sophie gets caught in the rain.

mathe-a21-08-matura:1.text:
Sophie's friend David was less lucky. He failed the written Matura: “Nicht genügend”. But there's a second chance, the compensation exam. It's oral and takes place three weeks later.

David prepares well. He makes a study plan: every day he studies one topic. For each topic he writes a short summary. Sophie helps him, because four years' worth of material is a lot.

On the day of the exam David is nervous. The examiner asks him three questions about functions and probability. He explains his working calmly and precisely. After twenty minutes the examiner smiles: “Passed, Mr Novak!” David is very relieved.

gloss.später: later (drei Wochen später — three weeks later)

questions: What kind of exam is the compensation exam?
What does David write for each topic?
How many questions does the examiner ask?

wrong: He carries out a work plan.

mathe-a21-09-textaufgaben:0.text:
Jakob hates word problems. Today the problem says: “A garden is twelve metres long and eight metres wide. A fence is to go around the garden. How many metres of fence do you need?”

Ms Berger gives tips: “Read the problem twice. Underline all the numbers. Then write down what is given and what you have to find.” Jakob writes: given are the length, twelve metres, and the width, eight metres. To find: the perimeter.

Then he makes a sketch: a rectangle with the numbers. Now he sees the approach: perimeter equals two times length plus two times width. He calculates: 24 plus 16 is 40. At the end he writes an answer sentence: “You need 40 metres of fence.” That wasn't so hard at all!

gloss.kommen: to come; (here) to be put up
gloss.gar: at all (gar nicht — not at all)

questions: What do you have to find?
What sketch does Jakob make?
How many metres of fence do you need?

translate.tr: At the end he writes an answer sentence.
wrong: At the beginning he writes an answer sentence.
At the end he makes a sketch.

mathe-a21-09-textaufgaben:1.text:
On Saturday Lea and her father cycle along the Danube to Krems. The distance is 45 kilometres. Their speed is about 18 kilometres per hour. How long is the journey?

First Lea estimates in her head: 45 divided by 20 is a bit more than two. So they'll need about two hours, maybe a bit more. Then she calculates exactly: 45 divided by 18 is 2.5. So the intermediate result is two and a half hours. Lea converts the hours into minutes: that's 150 minutes.

Her father calculates too, but he makes a mistake and gets 25 hours. Lea laughs: “Dad, that doesn't make sense! We're not that slow.”
questions: How long is the distance to Krems?
How long is the journey time?
Why does Lea laugh?

translate.tr: Lea converts the hours into minutes.
wrong: Lea converts the minutes into hours.
Lea counts the hours and minutes.

mathe-a21-10-studium:0.text:
After the Matura Sophie wants to study technical mathematics at TU Wien. The programme is a bachelor's with six semesters. For admission she registers online and sends her Matura certificate.

The winter semester starts in October. But already in September there's a preparatory maths course for first-year students. There they go over the material from school: functions, equations and vectors.

On the first day the lecture hall is full; more than three hundred people are sitting there. David is sitting next to Sophie. He isn't studying technical mathematics but training to teach maths and physics. Later he wants to teach at a school. Sophie is glad: she already knows someone.
questions: How many semesters does the bachelor's have?
When is the preparatory course?
What is David studying?

translate.tr: For admission you need the Matura.
wrong: For the Matura you need admission.
For admission you don't need the Matura.

translate.tr: The preparatory course is for first-year students.
wrong: The preparatory course is for teachers.
The lecture is for first-year students.

mathe-a21-10-studium:1.text:
The first weeks at university are demanding. Every lecture comes with lecture notes of two hundred pages. And every week there's a new problem sheet with five problems.

The deadline is always Monday at ten o'clock. Anyone who hands in the sheet too late gets no points. Sophie works together with David, but each of them writes their own solutions.

On Thursday there's the exercise group. The tutor is called Ahmed and is in his fifth semester. Sophie has to present a solution on the board. She's nervous, but Ahmed helps her. After the class he says: “It's hard for everyone at the beginning. A good mathematician doesn't give up quickly.”
questions: When is the deadline for the problem sheet?
Who is Ahmed?
What does Sophie have to do in the exercise group?

translate.tr: Every week there's a new problem sheet.
wrong: Every month there's a new problem sheet.

translate.tr: Anyone who hands in too late gets no points.
wrong: Anyone who hands in early gets more points.
Anyone who hands in late gets half the points.

cyber-a22-vorfaelle:0.text:
Jonas studies computer science at TU Wien and is doing an internship in a company's IT department. On Monday his boss Petra showed him a log file. During the night the traffic was very high, but nobody was in the office.

Petra said: “That's suspicious. We have to investigate the incident.” Together they read the log file. They saw that an unknown IP address had tested lots of ports. One port was open because a colleague hadn't closed it.

Jonas wanted to know whether the attacker had stolen data. Luckily the firewall stopped the connection. Petra blocked the IP address immediately and closed the port. Then she reported the incident.
questions: Where is Jonas doing an internship?
Why was the traffic suspicious?
Why was a port open?
What did Petra do at the end?

translate.tr: We have to investigate the incident.
wrong: We have to report the incident.
We don't have to investigate the incident.

translate.tr: At night the traffic was very high.
wrong: During the day the traffic was very high.
At night the traffic was very low.

cyber-a22-vorfaelle:1.text:
After the incident the company wrote a new security policy. Petra explained to Jonas why it's so important: “Many employees had too many permissions. That was a big risk.”

From now on only the administrator assigns the rights. Each employee only gets the permissions they need for their work. If someone wants more access, they have to submit a request.

Jonas was supposed to check whether everyone follows the rules. On the very first day he found a breach: a colleague had written his password on a piece of paper. Petra wasn't angry, but she said: “With good rules we can prevent many attacks. But it only works if everyone takes part.”

gloss.mitmachen: to take part, to join in

questions: What was the big risk?
Who assigns the rights from now on?
What do you have to do if you want more access?
What breach did Jonas find?

translate.tr: Only the administrator assigns the rights.
wrong: Only the administrator receives the rights.

translate.tr: Everyone has to follow the rules.
wrong: Everyone has to know the rules.
Everyone has to write the rules.

translate.tr: That was a breach of the security policy.
wrong: That was a change to the security policy.
That wasn't a breach of the security policy.

cyber-a22-02-kryptografie:0.text:
Sofia is in her third semester at TU Wien. On Tuesday she had the exercise class “Cryptography” for the first time. The tutor, Daniel, first explained symmetric encryption: an algorithm turns the plaintext into ciphertext. Anyone who has the same key can decrypt the ciphertext again.

“But how does the other person get the key?” Sofia asked. “If you send it by email, someone can steal it.” Daniel laughed: “That's exactly the problem.”

That's why there are also asymmetric methods. Each person has a key pair: a public key and a private key. Everyone may see the public key; the private one stays secret. With these keys two computers securely exchange a shared key at the start. After that, encryption is fast and symmetric.

gloss.mal: time (zum ersten Mal — for the first time)
gloss.schickt: sends (wenn man schickt — if you send)
gloss.gesehen: seen (darf gesehen werden — may be seen)
gloss.gar: at all (gar nicht — not at all)

questions: What does an algorithm do in encryption?
What problem does Sofia see?
Who may see the public key?
How is data encrypted after the exchange?

wrong: First we don't exchange a key.

translate.tr: Only with the key can you decrypt the ciphertext.
wrong: Only with the key can you encrypt the ciphertext.
Only with the key can you decrypt the plaintext.
You can decrypt the ciphertext even without the key.

translate.tr: Each person has their own key pair.
wrong: Each person has a shared key.
Not every person has a key pair.

cyber-a22-02-kryptografie:1.text:
At the weekend Sofia wanted to install Linux on her old laptop. She downloaded the file from an unknown website because the download was faster there. But the official site showed a hash value. Sofia computed the hash of her file and compared the two. They weren't the same!

On Monday she told Daniel about it. “Good thing you checked,” he said. “Someone probably tampered with the file. The hash shows whether the integrity of the data is intact.”

Then he explained the signature: the developers sign the hash with their private key. With the public key anyone can check the authenticity. But how do you know the public key is genuine? A certificate authority confirms that. “And confidential data?” Sofia asked. “You have to encrypt that as well,” Daniel answered.
questions: Why did Sofia download the file from an unknown website?
What did Sofia notice when comparing?
What do the developers sign the hash with?
Who confirms that a public key is genuine?

wrong: Someone will tamper with the file.

translate.tr: The signature proves the file's authenticity.
wrong: The signature proves the file's integrity.
The hash proves the file's authenticity.
The signature doesn't prove the file's authenticity.

cyber-a22-03-malware:0.text:
Elias studies computer science at TU Wien and works part-time in a school's IT support. Last week a teacher came to him with his laptop. The laptop was very slow, and unknown programs started by themselves.

Elias quickly found the reason: the teacher had downloaded a free program. It posed as a useful tool, but it was a Trojan. In the background there was also a keylogger running that recorded all the passwords.

During the break Elias explained the differences to a colleague: “A worm spreads over the network on its own. A Trojan has to be installed by the user.” But the most dangerous is ransomware: it encrypts all the files, and the attackers demand a ransom. Luckily the laptop was only infected with the Trojan.
questions: Where does Elias work part-time?
What did the program pose as?
What did the keylogger do?
What was the laptop infected with?

translate.tr: The worm spreads over the network.
wrong: The virus spreads over the network.
The worm spread over the network.
The worm doesn't spread over the network.

translate.tr: The laptop was infected with a Trojan.
wrong: The laptop wasn't infected with a Trojan.
The laptop was infected with a worm.

cyber-a22-03-malware:1.text:
The next day Ms Novak, the head of IT support, showed Elias her tools. “Why didn't the virus scanner detect the Trojan?” Elias asked. “Because the malicious code was brand new,” she answered. “The scanner didn't know it yet.”

That's why modern programs also look at a file's behaviour. Unknown files are first started in a sandbox. There they can't do any damage. If a file is suspicious, it goes into quarantine.

After that they had to clean the laptop. But Ms Novak was careful: “Maybe the Trojan opened a backdoor. Then the system will never be secure again.” So they reinstalled everything, and the teacher had to change all his passwords.

gloss.achten: pay attention (achten auf — to look at)

questions: Why didn't the virus scanner detect the Trojan?
What happens first to unknown files?
Why did they reinstall everything?
What did the teacher have to do at the end?

translate.tr: The virus scanner detected the malicious code.
wrong: The virus scanner deleted the malicious code.
The virus scanner didn't detect the malicious code.

translate.tr: We have to clean the laptop.
wrong: We have to switch off the laptop.
We don't have to clean the laptop.
We had to clean the laptop.

cyber-a22-04-websicherheit:0.text:
Nina and Lukas study computer science at TU Wien. For a project they programmed a small website where students can sell old books. On the home page there's a form with an input field for searching.

Before the site went online, Lukas wanted to test it. He typed a quotation mark into the input field and clicked on “Suchen”. An error message from the database appeared immediately. “That's bad,” he said. “SQL injection is possible here. An attacker can inject their own commands into our query.”

Nina was surprised, because she had filtered the input. But her filter was too simple. The better solution: you must never put input directly into the query. You have to escape special characters or use prepared statements.
questions: What can students do on the website?
What did Lukas type into the input field?
Why was Nina surprised?
What is the better solution?

translate.tr: Lukas typed a quotation mark into the input field.
wrong: Lukas typed a password into the input field.
Lukas types a quotation mark into the input field.
Nina typed a quotation mark into the input field.

translate.tr: We have to filter all input.
wrong: We have to save all input.
We don't have to filter the input.

translate.tr: The attacker injects commands into the database.
wrong: The attacker deletes commands from the database.
The administrator injects commands into the database.
The attacker injected commands into the database.

cyber-a22-04-websicherheit:1.text:
A week later the web application was already running. After logging in, every user got a session with a secret session ID. The browser sends this ID along with every request to the server.

Lukas found another problem: in the comments under the books you could write HTML. He tested a small script, and the browser really did run it. That way a malicious user can steal other people's session IDs and take over their sessions. Attacks like this are called cross-site scripting.

Nina fixed the comments right away. They also set sessions to expire after thirty minutes without activity. “A secure web application is more work than I thought,” said Nina. Lukas laughed: “But now we know how attackers think.”

gloss.später: later (eine Woche später — a week later)

questions: When does the browser send the session ID along?
Where did Lukas find the second problem?
What can a malicious user do with the session ID?
When does a session expire now?

translate.tr: The attacker has taken over the session.
wrong: The attacker has ended the session.
The attacker will take over the session.

translate.tr: The session expires after thirty minutes.
wrong: The session starts after thirty minutes.
The session expires after three minutes.
The session expired thirty minutes ago.

cyber-a22-05-authentifizierung:0.text:
Miriam is in her third semester at TU Wien. Since October she has been working ten hours a week at the university helpdesk. On her very first day a student came to her because he couldn't log in.

“Are your login credentials correct?” Miriam asked. The student was sure his password was right. But the one-time password from the app was no longer valid. A code like that expires after thirty seconds.

Miriam explained to him how authentication works: first the system checks the password, then the code. The code shows that he really has the phone. Only then is a token created. With this token the browser can show that his identity has already been verified.

The student tried again, faster this time. It worked.
questions: Where does Miriam work alongside her studies?
Why couldn't the student log in?
What does the system check first?
When is a token created?

translate.tr: The one-time password is no longer valid.
wrong: The one-time password is still valid.
The token is no longer valid.

translate.tr: The code expires after a short time.
wrong: The code arrives after a short time.
The code expired after a short time.

translate.tr: The system checks the login credentials first.
wrong: The system checks the login credentials later.
The system saves the login credentials first.

cyber-a22-05-authentifizierung:1.text:
After a month Miriam got a new task. She was to help teaching staff who had no access to their courses. For that she needed more access rights than before.

Her boss, Mr Novak, explained the difference to her: “Authentication shows who you are. Authorisation determines what you're allowed to do.” In the system every user has a role, for example student, lecturer or admin. Rights are assigned to a role, not to individual people.

Miriam had to request the new rights in writing and show her ID. Mr Novak said: “We follow the principle of least privilege. Your role stays restricted: you can see courses, but you can't change grades.” Miriam thought that made sense. That way the damage is smaller if an account is stolen.
questions: Why did Miriam need more access rights?
What does authorisation determine?
To what are rights assigned in the system?
What can't Miriam do with her role?

translate.tr: Every user has a role in the system.
wrong: Every user has a password in the system.
Not every user has a role in the system.

translate.tr: Miriam has to request the rights in writing.
wrong: Miriam has to grant the rights in writing.
Miriam has to request the rights verbally.
Her role is no longer restricted.

cyber-a22-06-penetrationstest:0.text:
Aylin studies computer science at TU Wien and is doing an internship at a small security company. This week the company got a new commission: a bakery with an online shop wanted a penetration test.

Aylin wanted to start right away, but her colleague Stefan said: “Without a contract we can't do anything. Otherwise a pentest is just an ordinary attack, and that's illegal.”

First the scope was agreed with the bakery. The contract says exactly which target systems will be tested: the online shop and the web server. The till system in the branches isn't included. The time is fixed too: testing only takes place at night, from Monday to Friday.

On Thursday the boss's signature finally arrived. From that moment the test was allowed, and Aylin could begin.

gloss.ab: from (ab diesem Moment — from this moment)

questions: What did the bakery want?
Why wasn't Aylin allowed to start right away?
What isn't included in the scope?
When is testing allowed?

translate.tr: Without a contract the test isn't allowed.
wrong: With a contract the test isn't allowed.
Without a contract the test is allowed.

translate.tr: We agreed on the scope exactly.
wrong: We're agreeing on the scope exactly.

translate.tr: The company got a new commission.
wrong: The company got a new contract.
The company sent a new commission.

cyber-a22-06-penetrationstest:1.text:
On the first night Aylin scanned the web server. She found that an old version of the shop software was running. With a simple trick she could see other customers' orders. Stefan said: “We have to prove it, but we mustn't copy any real data.” So they only took screenshots.

After that they wrote the report. At the beginning there's a short summary for the boss, who isn't a technician. Then each vulnerability is described, and each gets a severity: low, medium, high or critical. The hole in the shop got the highest severity.

At the end of each point there's a recommendation, for example: “Update the software immediately.” The report is confidential and was sent to the bakery encrypted.
questions: What did Aylin find on the web server?
Why did they only take screenshots?
Who is the summary for?
What severity did the hole in the shop get?

translate.tr: At the end there's a recommendation.
wrong: At the beginning there's a recommendation.
At the end there's a summary.

cyber-a22-07-incident-response:0.text:
Lukas studies business informatics and works part-time at a logistics company in Vienna. On Friday at seven in the morning, half the computers in the warehouse were suddenly locked. A message from blackmailers was on the screens. There was an outage: nobody could send parcels.

His team leader, Ms Berger, immediately opened the emergency plan. It described exactly what to do. The first immediate action was clear: the affected computers had to be isolated. Lukas disconnected them from the network so that the malware couldn't spread any further.

“First we contain the attack, then we look for the cause,” said Ms Berger. After two hours the attack was contained. Luckily the servers at headquarters weren't affected.
questions: What was on the screens?
What was the first immediate action?
Why did Lukas disconnect the computers from the network?
Which systems weren't affected?

wrong: The affected computers have to be switched off.
The affected computers don't have to be isolated.

cyber-a22-07-incident-response:1.text:
The following week the forensics began. An external expert helped the team analyse the log files. He looked for traces of the attacker and made a list: at what time was the attacker in the network, and which computers did he use?

The trail led to an email. An employee had opened a fake attachment. Luckily the scale was smaller than feared: no customer data was stolen.

The computers in the warehouse were reinstalled, and after three days everything was running normally again. At the end the team met to learn lessons from the incident. Ms Berger said: “We have to get better at preventing attacks like this. From now on there will be training for everyone every month.”

gloss.ziehen: to draw (Lehren ziehen — to learn lessons)

questions: Who helped the team with the forensics?
How did the attacker get into the network?
How big was the scale?
What will there be every month from now on?

wrong: The expert deletes the log files.
The expert analysed the log files.

translate.tr: We have to prevent attacks like this.
wrong: We have to investigate attacks like this.
We can't prevent attacks like this.

cyber-a22-08-datenschutzrecht:0.text:
Selin studies business informatics at TU Wien. In the summer she's working at a small start-up that's developing an app for gyms. In her first week the lawyer, Ms Hofbauer, explained the GDPR to her.

“Our app processes personal data: names, email addresses and training times,” said Ms Hofbauer. “In terms of the GDPR, our company is the controller. The customers are the data subjects.”

Selin wanted to know whether you can simply collect all the data. “No,” the lawyer answered. “For every processing we need a legal basis, for example a contract or consent. We also have to define the purpose exactly. We can't use data for training for advertising.”

At the end Selin asked: “Is it permissible to store the data forever?” — “No. Only as long as necessary for the purpose.”

In terms of the GDPR, who is the controller?
What do you need for every processing?
How long may the data be stored?

wrong: The app doesn't process personal data.

translate.tr: We need a legal basis for the processing.
wrong: We need consent for the processing.
We don't need a legal basis for the processing.

translate.tr: We have to define the purpose exactly.
wrong: We can define the purpose exactly.
We have to define the time limit exactly.
We had to define the purpose exactly.

cyber-a22-08-datenschutzrecht:1.text:
Two months later there was a problem. An employee had sent a spreadsheet with customer data to the wrong email address. Ms Hofbauer said immediately: “That's a data breach. We have to inform the data protection officer.”

The data protection officer examined the case and reported it to the supervisory authority. In Austria that's the Data Protection Authority. If a company hides a breach, it can get a large fine.

A few days later a customer wrote to the start-up. She requested information about her data and then its deletion. She also objected to advertising by email. Selin was allowed to help with the reply.

Later Selin was to anonymise old training data for a statistic. “Without names it's no longer personal data,” Ms Hofbauer explained. “Then the statistic isn't a risk.”
questions: What did the employee do wrong?
Who reported the data breach to the supervisory authority?
What did the customer request?
Why should Selin anonymise the training data?
