wrong: We have to fix the data breach immediately.
We don't have to report the data breach immediately.
We have to report the data breach later.

translate.tr: The company can get a large fine.
wrong: The company has to get a large fine.
The company got a large fine.
The company can pay a small fine.

translate.tr: She requested information about her data.
wrong: She requested the deletion of her data.
He requested information about his data.
She's requesting information about her data.

cyber-a22-09-ctf:0.text:
Kerem is in his second semester at TU Wien. In the autumn his fellow student Mira asked him whether he wanted to take part in a CTF competition. CTF means “Capture the Flag”. Kerem had no experience, but he was curious.

Their team had four people and a funny name: “Die Wiener Würstchen” (The Vienna Sausages). On Saturday at nine o'clock the competition started. Each task was a puzzle from a different area: web, cryptography or reverse engineering. Whoever solves a puzzle finds a flag and has to submit it on the website.

They were stuck on one task for a long time. Then they bought a hint, but you lose points for that. The hint was good, and Mira was able to find the flag quickly.

At the end the team was in twelfth place on the leaderboard. “Not bad for the first time!” said Mira.
questions: What does CTF mean?
What do you have to do with a flag?
What happens if you buy a hint?
What place was the team in at the end?

translate.tr: We want to take part in a competition.
wrong: We want to win a competition.
We don't want to take part in a competition.
We took part in a competition.
Our team didn't submit the flag.

cyber-a22-09-ctf:1.text:
After the competition Kerem wanted to learn more about binary exploitation. Mira recommended a learning platform to him. There you get a binary and have to find a vulnerability.

The first task was a simple buffer overflow. Kerem opened the program in the debugger and watched the memory. He tried lots of inputs, but his exploit didn't work. For two evenings he couldn't find the mistake.

Mira said: “You have to keep at it. At the beginning everything takes a long time.” On the third evening Kerem finally found the mistake: the address in the exploit was wrong. After that his exploit showed the flag.

Now Kerem writes down how he solved each task. That way he sees his progress, and later he can go over everything again.

gloss.lang: for (zwei Abende lang — for two evenings)

questions: What do you get on the learning platform?
What did Kerem use to watch the memory?
Why didn't the exploit work at first?
Why does Kerem write down how he solved the tasks?

translate.tr: He tried the exploit in the debugger.
wrong: He wrote the exploit in the debugger.
He'll try the exploit in the debugger.
She tried the exploit in the debugger.

translate.tr: You have to keep at it.
wrong: We have to keep at it.

translate.tr: The first task was a buffer overflow.
wrong: The last task was a buffer overflow.
The first task was an exploit.

cyber-a22-10-beruf:0.text:
Elias studied at TU Wien and has been working for a year as an analyst in a Security Operations Center, SOC for short. The SOC monitors the networks of many companies. Because attacks happen at night too, the analysts work in three shifts.

Last week Elias was on night shift. At two o'clock an alert came: a server had suddenly sent a lot of data to the outside. Elias had to analyse the events carefully. He read the log files and found the reason: a new backup program had copied the data to the cloud. So it was only a false alarm.

An hour later he saw something dangerous. Someone was trying to log in a hundred times with wrong passwords. Elias couldn't solve this problem on his own. So he escalated the case to his team leader immediately.
questions: Why do the analysts work in shifts?
What was the reason for the first alert?
What did Elias see an hour later?
What did Elias do with the second case?

translate.tr: The SOC monitors the networks of many companies.
wrong: The SOC protects the networks of many companies.
The SOC monitored the networks of many companies.
The SOC doesn't monitor the networks of many companies.

translate.tr: It was only a false alarm.

cyber-a22-10-beruf:1.text:
Elias likes telling how he got his job. While he was still studying he took part in CTF competitions. After that he did an internship in an IT department. That way he had a bit of work experience.

In his last semester he applied to five companies. In his application he described his knowledge of Linux and networks. Two companies invited him to an interview.

In the interview the boss above all wanted to know how he solves problems. She also asked whether he had a certification. Elias didn't have one yet, but now the company is paying for it.

At first Elias was surprised by the salary, because it was higher than he had thought. His tip for students: “Don't just study for exams. Show in your application what you've done in real projects.”
questions: How did Elias gain work experience?
How many companies invited him to an interview?
What did the boss want to know above all?
Who is paying for the certification?

translate.tr: For this position you need good knowledge of Linux.
wrong: For this position you need experience with Linux.
For this position you don't need knowledge of Linux.

translate.tr: Tomorrow I have a job interview.
wrong: Yesterday I had a job interview.
Tomorrow he has a job interview.

informatik-a22-code:0.text:
Lena is in her first semester of computer science at TU Wien. This week she had to write her first program in Python. The task was a simple algorithm: the program should find the largest number in a list.

First Lena wrote a loop. The loop goes through all the values in the list. Inside the loop there's a condition: if a value is bigger than the maximum, it becomes the new maximum.

Then she entered a command in the terminal and ran the program. But there was an error, because one number in the list was stored as text. Her tutor Paul read the source code and said: “The data type is wrong. You have to convert the text into a number first.”
questions: What should Lena's program find?
What is inside the loop?
Why was there an error?
Who read the source code?

translate.tr: The loop goes through all the values.
wrong: The loop goes through some of the values.
The condition goes through all the values.

informatik-a22-code:1.text:
In the second week Lena wrote a program in C. Before you can run it, you have to compile it. Lena's IDE didn't show any error, but the program still crashed.

Lena didn't know whether the problem was with the input or the output. So she tested the program with different inputs. With small numbers the output was correct. But with very big numbers the program crashed.

Paul explained to her that the data type int is too small for such big numbers. Lena fixed the bug and wrote a comment in the source code. Now everyone knows why it says long there.
questions: What do you have to do before you run a program in C?
When did the program crash?
How did Lena test the program?
What did Lena write in the source code?

translate.tr: With small numbers the output was correct.
wrong: With big numbers the output was correct.
With small numbers the input was correct.
With small numbers the output was wrong.

informatik-a22-02-datenstrukturen:0.text:
Mira studies computer science at TU Wien. Last week in the course “Algorithms and Data Structures” she had to build a simple data structure: a list with the names of all the students in her exercise group.

At first Mira wanted to use an array. But an array has a fixed length, and the group kept getting bigger. So she used a list instead, because its length can change.

Every element in the list has an index. The first index is zero, not one. At first that seemed strange to Mira. With the index you can access an element directly.

After that she had to sort the names alphabetically. Her fellow student Jonas showed her that Python already has a ready-made function for that.
questions: Why didn't Mira use an array?
Which index does a list start with?
What did Mira have to do after that?
Who helped Mira?

translate.tr: An array has a fixed length.
wrong: A list has a fixed length.
An array doesn't have a fixed length.

translate.tr: She had to sort the names.
wrong: She had to delete the names.
He had to sort the names.
She'll have to sort the names.

informatik-a22-02-datenstrukturen:1.text:
The next session was about more data structures. The professor started with an everyday example: in the canteen there's a stack of plates. You always take the top plate. A stack in a computer works the same way: the last element is removed first.

With a queue it's the other way round. Whoever comes first is served first — like at the checkout in a supermarket.

Then she drew a tree on the board. At the very top was the root, and below it came more nodes. Each node had a pointer to its children.

Jonas asked: “Why do you need a tree like that?” The professor answered: “You can search a sorted tree much faster than a long list.”

gloss.ging: went (es ging um — it was about)

questions: What everyday example does the professor give for a stack?
How does a queue work?
What was at the very top of the tree?
Why do you need a sorted tree?

translate.tr: The last element is removed first.
wrong: The last element is added first.

translate.tr: At the very top is the root.
wrong: At the very bottom is the root.
At the very top is a node.

informatik-a22-03-objektorientierung:0.text:
In their second semester Aylin and Tobias are learning Java. In the first exercise class they had to write a class Fahrrad (bicycle). The idea was simple: a class is like a blueprint, and an object is a specific bicycle built from this plan.

Every bicycle has attributes, for example colour and speed. The class also has methods, such as braking or going faster.

To create a new object you need a constructor. Aylin gave the constructor two parameters: the colour and the number of the bike. Then she created three bicycles and called the method bremsen (brake) for each one.

Tobias was unsure at first because he didn't know the terms. But after the exercise class he could explain everything.
questions: According to the text, what is a class?
What parameters does Aylin's constructor have?
How many bicycles did Aylin create?
Why was Tobias unsure at first?

translate.tr: An object is a specific bicycle.
wrong: A class is a specific bicycle.
An object isn't a specific bicycle.

translate.tr: The constructor creates a new object.
wrong: The constructor deletes a new object.
The constructor creates a new class.

informatik-a22-03-objektorientierung:1.text:
A week later came the next task: Aylin and Tobias had to write a subclass Elektrofahrrad (e-bike). An e-bike is also a bicycle, so it can inherit from the superclass Fahrrad. That way you don't have to write the code again.

Through inheritance the e-bike immediately had all the attributes and methods. Tobias only had to override the method for going faster, because an e-bike has a motor.

Then the tutor explained the principle of encapsulation: the attributes are private, and you can only change them via methods. The method for the battery has a return value: it returns the charge level in per cent.

“At first it was all very abstract,” said Aylin, “but now I understand what it's for.”

gloss.später: later (eine Woche später — a week later)
gloss.gar: at all (gar nicht — not at all)

questions: Which class does the e-bike inherit from?
Which method did Tobias have to override?
How can you change private attributes?
What does the method for the battery return?

translate.tr: The subclass inherits all the methods.
wrong: The superclass inherits all the methods.
The subclass inherits some of the methods.

translate.tr: Tobias had to override the method.
wrong: Tobias had to call the method.
Tobias didn't have to override the method.

informatik-a22-04-versionsverwaltung:0.text:
In the summer Felix is doing an internship at a small software company in Vienna. On the first day his colleague Sara explained to him how the team works with version control.

All the code is in one repository. When someone changes something, they save the change with a commit. Every commit has a short message so that the others know what happened.

In the history you can see all the commits: who changed something and when. With a command you can compare two versions.

In the afternoon Felix made a mistake, and the app wouldn't start any more. He was nervous, but Sara stayed calm: “No problem, we'll just roll the code back to the last state.” After a minute everything worked again.
questions: Where is all the code?
Why does every commit have a message?
What can you see in the history?
What did Sara do after the mistake?

translate.tr: Every commit has a short message.
wrong: Every commit has a long message.
Every repository has a short message.

informatik-a22-04-versionsverwaltung:1.text:
In the second week Felix got his first task of his own. First he had to clone the repository, that is, get a copy onto his laptop. Then he created a new branch, because only tested code should ever go on the main branch.

Sara was working on the same file at the same time, but in a different branch. When Felix wanted to merge his branch into the main branch, there was a conflict: they had both changed the same line.

Felix didn't know which version was right. Together with Sara he resolved the conflict. After that a third colleague did a code review and found two more small mistakes. Only then were the changes taken into the main branch.
questions: What does “klonen” mean in the text?
Why was there a conflict?
Who did the code review?
What code should go on the main branch?

translate.tr: Felix had to clone the repository.
wrong: Felix had to delete the repository.
Felix didn't have to clone the repository.

translate.tr: Sara was working in a different branch at the same time.
wrong: Sara was working in a different branch later.
Sara was working in the same branch at the same time.

informatik-a22-05-webentwicklung:0.text:
Jonas studies computer science at TU Wien and is doing an internship at a small start-up. The company is developing a web application for rental bikes in Vienna. On the first day his colleague Mira explained to him how the web works.

“When you open the page, the client sends a request to the server,” she said. “The request is processed by the server, and then a response comes back. The response always contains a status code. If something is missing, you see the well-known error ‘Not Found’.”

After that Mira showed him the company's API. It has lots of endpoints: one endpoint delivers the available bikes, another the prices. Jonas was allowed to write a request himself. At first he was nervous, but the response came immediately.

gloss.vom: by the (vom Server — by the server)

questions: Where is Jonas doing an internship?
What does the response always contain?
What does one of the API's endpoints deliver?
How did Jonas feel at first?

translate.tr: The client sends a request to the server.
wrong: The server sends a request to the client.
The client sends a response to the server.

translate.tr: The response contains a status code.
wrong: The request contains a status code.
The response doesn't contain a status code.

informatik-a22-05-webentwicklung:1.text:
After two weeks Jonas got his first task of his own. The bike page took too long to load, and sometimes the page didn't respond at all.

Mira works on the back end; her colleague Daniel is responsible for the front end. The front end was built with a modern framework. It fetches the data via the API and displays it as a map.

Jonas found the problem quickly: with every click the front end fetched all the bikes in Vienna, not just the bikes nearby. On top of that, the back end sent the data in a very large format. Together with Mira, Jonas changed both parts. After that the page loaded in one second, and the boss was happy.

gloss.gar: at all (gar nicht — not at all)

questions: What was the problem with the bike page?
Who is responsible for the front end?
What data did the front end fetch with every click?
How long did loading take afterwards?

translate.tr: The front end displays the data as a map.
wrong: The back end displays the data as a map.
The front end saves the data as a map.

translate.tr: The page's loading time was too long.
wrong: The page's loading time was too short.
The page's loading time is too long.

translate.tr: The page doesn't respond to my click.
wrong: The page responds to my click.
The page doesn't respond to his click.

informatik-a22-06-sql:0.text:
Selin is in her third semester of business informatics at TU Wien. In the database exercise class the students learn SQL, the best-known query language.

The tutor, Katharina, had prepared a table with all the books in the university library. Every row had a primary key, and the columns held the title, author and year. The first task was easy: you only had to select the title and the year.

Then it got harder. Selin had to filter all the books by year and sort the result in ascending order. Her first query was wrong because she had forgotten WHERE. So the result was far too long. On the second try everything worked, and Selin was proud.

gloss.stand: stood; (in der Tabelle stand) was in the table
gloss.name: name

questions: What data had Katharina prepared?
What was in the columns?
What did Selin have to filter the books by?
Why was the first query wrong?

translate.tr: Every row has a primary key.
wrong: Every row has a foreign key.
Every column has a primary key.

translate.tr: Selin had to filter the books by year.
wrong: Selin had to sort the books by year.
Selin had to filter the books by author.

informatik-a22-06-sql:1.text:
The following week was about several tables. Katharina explained: “If you write all the data into a single table, you get redundancy. An author's name, for example, then appears in the table a hundred times.”

So the students had to design a new schema. Authors and books went into two separate tables. There's a relationship between the tables: every book has a foreign key that points to the author number. This number of course has to be unique.

At the end Selin had to join the two tables with JOIN and group the books by author. For some books the author field contained a null value, because the author was unknown. These books were missing from the result, and Selin had to find out why.

gloss.ging: went (es ging um — it was about)
gloss.name: name

questions: What happens if all the data is in one table?
What does the foreign key point to?
What did Selin have to use to join the tables?
Why were some books missing from the result?

translate.tr: There's a relationship between the tables.
wrong: There's no relationship between the tables.
There's a relationship between the columns.

translate.tr: The number has to be unique.
Selin grouped the books by author.
wrong: Selin sorted the books by author.
Selin grouped the books by year.

informatik-a22-07-betriebssysteme:0.text:
Tobias and Aylin are studying together for the operating systems exam. Suddenly Tobias's laptop became very slow, and the fan was loud.

Aylin opened the terminal and typed the command top. Now they could see all the processes. One process was using almost all the CPU time: an old program that Tobias had forgotten about. “It's running with high priority and using all the cores at the same time,” Aylin explained.

Tobias wanted to know whether a process can do several tasks at once. “Yes, that's what threads are for,” said Aylin. “A process can have lots of threads, and the operating system distributes them across the cores.” Then she killed the process with the command kill. After a few seconds the laptop was fast again.
questions: What was wrong with Tobias's laptop?
Which process was using almost all the CPU time?
What does the operating system distribute across the cores?
What did Aylin use to kill the process?

translate.tr: A process can have many threads.
wrong: A process can have only one thread.
A process has to have many threads.

translate.tr: The process is running with high priority.
wrong: The process is running with low priority.
The process was running with high priority.

informatik-a22-07-betriebssysteme:1.text:
The next day the lecture was about memory management. The professor explained that every process gets its own virtual memory. The operating system allocates memory to it, and when the process ends, the memory is freed again. A process mustn't simply read another process's memory.

After that she talked about the file system. Files are in directories, and every file has a path that shows where it is. Every file also has permissions: they determine who may read or change the file.

In the exercise class Tobias wanted to open a file in another user's directory. The system only showed an error message because he didn't have permission. Aylin laughed: “That's not a bug, that's security!”

gloss.ging: went (es ging um — it was about)

questions: What does every process get?
What happens to the memory when the process ends?
What do permissions determine?
Why did the system show an error message?

translate.tr: The operating system allocates memory to the process.
wrong: The operating system frees the process's memory.
The process allocates memory to the operating system.

translate.tr: Tobias didn't have permission for the file.
wrong: Tobias had permission for the file.
Tobias doesn't have permission for the file.

informatik-a22-08-netzwerke:0.text:
Last week in the course “Computer Networks” at TU Wien, Jonas had to answer a question: how does a message get from his laptop to a server in Graz?

The professor explained it like this: the message isn't transmitted as a whole. It's split into lots of small packets. Each packet has a header with the IP address of the sender and of the receiver. There's also a port, so that the receiver knows which program gets the data.

A network works in layers, and each layer has its own protocol. The checksum shows whether a packet was damaged on the way. Jonas found it difficult at first, but after the exercise class it was clear to him.
questions: Where does Jonas's message go?
What is in the header of every packet?
What do you need the port for?
What does the checksum show?

translate.tr: The message is split into packets.
wrong: The message isn't split into packets.
The file is split into packets.

translate.tr: Each layer has its own protocol.
wrong: Each packet has its own protocol.
All layers have the same protocol.

informatik-a22-08-netzwerke:1.text:
On Thursday Jonas and his fellow student Mira were in the networking lab. There are several switches there, and each computer is a node in the network. First they had to draw the topology: which nodes are directly connected?

Then Mira sent packets to a computer at the other end. Each switch forwards the packets until they reach their destination. At first the delay was very small. When Jonas pulled out a cable, some packets got lost.

The tutor explained: “The TCP protocol is reliable. The receiver sends an acknowledgement for every packet. If the acknowledgement is missing, the packet is sent again.” UDP has no acknowledgements, but in return it's faster.
questions: What did Jonas and Mira have to do first?
What happened when Jonas pulled out a cable?
Why is TCP reliable?

translate.tr: The protocol is reliable but slow.
wrong: The protocol is unreliable but fast.
The protocol is reliable and fast.

informatik-a22-09-softwareprojekt:0.text:
In the third semester at TU Wien there's a course in which students do a real software project. Selin's group has a client: Mr Berger has a small bakery in Ottakring and wants an app for orders.

At the first meeting the group gathered all the requirements. Mr Berger wanted a lot, but not everything was important. So the students described each use case precisely, for example: “A customer orders bread for Saturday.” Everything went into a requirements specification.

After that they defined the architecture and made a design of the interface. After two weeks they showed Mr Berger a simple prototype. He was pleased: “That's exactly how I imagined it. Can you implement it by June?”
questions: What does Mr Berger want?
Who is Selin's group's client?
Where did all the use cases go?
What did the students show after two weeks?

translate.tr: The group gathered all the requirements.
wrong: The group gathered some of the requirements.
The group fulfilled all the requirements.
The client gathered all the requirements.

translate.tr: The client was pleased with the prototype.
wrong: The client wasn't pleased with the prototype.
The client is pleased with the prototype.

informatik-a22-09-softwareprojekt:1.text:
The group worked in two-week sprints. At the start everyone estimated the effort for each feature. The estimate was often too optimistic, and some tasks took twice as long.

After every sprint Mr Berger gave feedback. Once he said: “The font is too small, my customers aren't young any more.” That way the app got better step by step.

In June came the acceptance. Mr Berger tested all the use cases and signed the report. Then the group could ship the app. Finally Selin wrote the documentation, because next year another group is taking over the maintenance. Without good documentation nobody understands the code.

gloss.doppelt: twice (doppelt so lange — twice as long)

questions: How long did a sprint last?
What was often the problem with the estimate?
What did Mr Berger say about the font?
Why did Selin write the documentation?

translate.tr: We estimate the effort for each feature.
wrong: We reduce the effort for each feature.
We estimated the effort for each feature.

translate.tr: After every sprint the client gave feedback.
wrong: Before every sprint the client gave feedback.
After every sprint the client gave no feedback.

informatik-a22-10-ki:0.text:
Amira studies computer science and works on a small project in the machine learning lab. Her model is supposed to recognise birds in photos, for example blackbirds and sparrows.

First Amira needed a good data set. Biology students had collected thousands of photos and noted the name of the bird on each photo. This training data was very valuable.

Then Amira trained the model. It learned by itself which features are important: the colour, the shape of the beak, the size. After that she tested the model with new photos it had never seen. At first the accuracy was only average, because many predictions were wrong. But with more data the model got noticeably better.
questions: What is Amira's model supposed to recognise?
Who collected the photos?
What did Amira test the model with?
How did the model get better?

translate.tr: Amira trained the model with lots of photos.
wrong: Amira tested the model with lots of photos.
Amira trained the model with a few photos.

translate.tr: At first the accuracy wasn't good.
wrong: At first the accuracy was good.
At the end the accuracy wasn't good.
The model doesn't recognise important features.

informatik-a22-10-ki:1.text:
In a seminar on artificial intelligence the students discussed opportunities and risks. Tobias showed how a chatbot works: behind it there's a large language model, that is, a neural network trained on huge amounts of text. It finds patterns in language and writes new sentences that way.

Then Amira talked about image recognition. A well-known system recognised the faces of people with light skin much better than the faces of people with dark skin. The reason was a bias in the data: there were almost only photos of light-skinned faces.

At the end the professor said: “You always have to analyse the results critically. A model is only as good as its data.”
questions: What is behind a chatbot?
What did the system recognise less well?
What was the reason for the problem?

translate.tr: A chatbot finds patterns in language.
wrong: A chatbot finds mistakes in language.
A chatbot doesn't find patterns in language.

translate.tr: The data had a strong bias.
wrong: The data had a weak bias.

translate.tr: We have to analyse the results critically.
wrong: We don't have to analyse the results critically.
We have to analyse the data critically.

mathe-a22-geometrie:0.text:
On Wednesday Sara had her first maths exercise class at TU Wien. The tutor wrote an equation on the board and asked who could solve it. At first Sara didn't want to, but then she went up to the front.

On the left-hand side there was a long expression. Sara simplified it first. Then she rearranged the equation until the unknown was on its own on one side. That's how she found the solution.

The tutor was pleased, but she asked: “Are you sure the solution is right?” Sara did a check. She substituted the solution into the equation, and both sides were equal. “The check only takes a minute, but it's very important,” said the tutor.

gloss.vorne: at the front (nach vorne — to the front)

questions: What was on the left-hand side?
What did Sara do first?
How did Sara check her answer?

translate.tr: The unknown is on its own on the left-hand side.
wrong: The unknown is on its own on the right-hand side.
The solution is on its own on the left-hand side.

mathe-a22-geometrie:1.text:
Sara lives in a shared flat in Vienna. Behind the house there's a small garden, and the flatmates want to plant vegetables there. Because Sara studies maths, she was supposed to plan everything.

The garden is a rectangle. Sara measured the length and the width and then calculated the area. For a fence she also needed the perimeter.

In one corner her flatmate Tim wanted a triangular bed. The angle in the corner is a right angle, so the area was easy to calculate: length times width, divided by two.

In the middle there's to be a round table. For the circle Sara needed the number pi. At the end Tim said: “So maths is useful after all!”
questions: What shape is the garden?
Why did Sara need the perimeter?
Why was the area of the triangle easy to calculate?
What is to go in the middle?

translate.tr: For the fence she needed the perimeter.
wrong: For the fence she needed the area.
For the table she needed the perimeter.

mathe-a22-02-folgen:0.text:
The first lecture of “Analysis 1” starts with sequences. Professor Weber writes on the board: a n equals one over n. “The first term is one, the second a half, the third a third. What happens as n tends to infinity?”

Sophie sees it right away: the terms keep getting smaller, the sequence is monotonically decreasing. It converges to zero, so the limit is zero. The sequence is also bounded, because all the terms lie between zero and one.

Then the professor shows a second example: a n equals n. “This sequence grows without end. It has no limit; it diverges.” At the end he says an important sentence: “Every convergent sequence is bounded. But not every bounded sequence converges.”

gloss.durch: over, divided by (eins durch n — one over n)
gloss.gegen: towards (n gegen unendlich — n tends to infinity)

questions: What is the limit of the sequence one over n?
What does the sequence a n = n do?
Which statement is correct?

translate.tr: All the terms lie between zero and one.
wrong: All the terms are greater than one.
Some terms lie between zero and one.

mathe-a22-02-folgen:1.text:
In the exercise class Sophie has to prove that one over n is a null sequence. She's unsure. The tutor, Marie, explains the definition: “A sequence converges to a if, for every arbitrary epsilon greater than zero, almost all terms lie in the epsilon-neighbourhood of a.”

“And how do I show that?” Sophie asks. Marie answers: “You bound the distance. We need the inequality: one over n is less than epsilon. That holds as soon as n is greater than one over epsilon.”

Sophie writes down the proof. Even if epsilon is very small, there's an n like that. So the terms really do tend to zero. Marie nods: “Exactly. And now the homework: find an upper bound for the sequence in problem three.”

gloss.durch: over (eins durch n — one over n)

questions: What does Sophie have to prove?
Who explains the definition?
What does Sophie have to find for homework?

wrong: The terms are equal to zero.

mathe-a22-03-ableitung:0.text:
Professor Weber starts with an example from physics. A car travels 160 kilometres in two hours. The average speed is 80 kilometres per hour. But how fast is the car going right now? That's the instantaneous rate of change.

“We make the time interval smaller and smaller,” Weber explains. “The limit is the derivative.” Geometrically the derivative is the slope of the tangent. The tangent touches the graph at exactly one point.

Then he differentiates some functions. For sine of two x you need the chain rule: the derivative is two times cosine of two x. At the end comes an important theorem: every differentiable function is continuous. The converse isn't true. The absolute value function is continuous, but at zero it has a kink and isn't differentiable there.
questions: What is the average speed?
What is the derivative geometrically?
Where is the absolute value function not differentiable?

translate.tr: The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change.
wrong: The derivative is the average rate of change.
The integral is the instantaneous rate of change.

translate.tr: Here we need the chain rule.
wrong: Here we don't need the chain rule.
Here we need the product rule.

mathe-a22-03-ableitung:1.text:
In the exercise class there's a typical optimisation problem: a farmer has twenty metres of fence and wants to build a rectangular garden with the largest possible area. What sides must the rectangle have?

Sophie sets up the function: A of x equals x times ten minus x. That's a parabola opening downwards. The zeros are zero and ten. To optimise the area, she differentiates and sets the derivative equal to zero. That's how she finds the point x equals five.

Is that a maximum or a minimum? The second derivative is negative, so it's a maximum. The maximum area is 25 square metres, and the garden is a square. Here there's only a minimum at the boundary. The parabola has no point of inflection.

gloss.setzt: sets (gleich null setzen — to set equal to zero)

questions: How much fence does the farmer have?
Why is x equals five a maximum?
How big is the maximum area?

translate.tr: She sets the derivative equal to zero.
wrong: She sets the function equal to one.

translate.tr: The parabola has no point of inflection.
wrong: The parabola has two points of inflection.

mathe-a22-04-integral:0.text:
Today the question is: how big is the area under the parabola x squared between zero and three? Professor Weber says: “This area is given by the definite integral. The lower limit is zero, the upper limit is three.”

To calculate the integral we need an antiderivative. That's a function whose derivative is x squared, for example x cubed over three. Any other antiderivative differs only by a constant C.

Then comes the fundamental theorem: you substitute the upper and the lower limit into the antiderivative and take the difference. Nine minus zero is nine. The professor smiles: “So differentiating and integrating are two sides of the same coin.”

gloss.hoch: to the power of (x hoch drei — x cubed)
gloss.durch: over, divided by (durch drei — over three)

questions: What is the upper limit?
How do two antiderivatives differ?
How big is the area?

translate.tr: The fundamental theorem connects the derivative and the integral.
wrong: The fundamental theorem separates the derivative and the integral.
The fundamental theorem connects the limit and the sequence.

mathe-a22-04-integral:1.text:
In the exercise class the tutor, Marie, shows where the integral comes from. She divides the interval from zero to three into three parts of equal width. That's a partition. Above each part she draws a rectangle.

If the rectangles stay under the graph, you get the lower sum: it's five and so too small. If they go above the graph, you get the upper sum: fourteen, so too big. The true area lies in between.

“And now we refine the partition,” says Marie. With a hundred parts both sums are already very close to nine. In the limit they're equal. Computers work the same way: they calculate integrals numerically. The result is only an approximation, but the accuracy is usually good enough in practice.
questions: How many parts does Marie divide the interval into at first?
How big is the lower sum?
What does a computer calculate?

translate.tr: The lower sum is too small.
wrong: The lower sum is too big.
The upper sum is too small.

translate.tr: The result is only an approximation.

mathe-a22-05-lineare-algebra:0.text:
In the first “Linear Algebra” lecture Professor Huber draws two arrows in a coordinate system. The first vector has the coordinates two and one, the second minus one and two.

“If I multiply a vector by a scalar, its length changes. With a negative scalar the direction changes too.” Then she calculates the dot product: two times minus one plus one times two. That's zero! So the two vectors are perpendicular to each other.

They're also linearly independent: neither is a multiple of the other. That's why they form a basis of the plane. The plane is a vector space of dimension two. Sophie writes it down: “Two independent vectors in the plane are always a basis.”
questions: What is the dot product of the two vectors?
When does the direction change?
What dimension does the plane have?

translate.tr: The vectors are perpendicular to each other.
wrong: The vectors are parallel to each other.
The vectors lie on one line.

translate.tr: A negative scalar changes the direction.
wrong: A positive scalar changes the direction.
A negative scalar doesn't change the direction.

mathe-a22-05-lineare-algebra:1.text:
The second week is about matrices. Professor Huber writes up a matrix with two rows and two columns: two and one at the top, one and three at the bottom. “Every matrix describes a linear map.”

First the class calculates the determinant: two times three minus one times one, so five. Because the determinant isn't zero, the matrix is invertible. It has full rank, namely two. That's why the corresponding system of equations has exactly one solution.

A student asks: “What happens if you transpose the matrix?” The professor answers: “With this matrix it stays the same, because it's symmetric. Symmetric matrices have nice properties. Next week we'll calculate their eigenvalues.”

gloss.schreibt: writes (anschreiben — to write up on the board)

questions: How big is the determinant?
Why is the matrix invertible?
What happens when you transpose it?

translate.tr: The system of equations has exactly one solution.
wrong: The system of equations has no solution.
The system of equations has infinitely many solutions.

translate.tr: Next week we'll calculate the eigenvalues.
wrong: Last week we calculated the eigenvalues.
Next week we'll calculate the determinant.

mathe-a22-06-logik:0.text:
The first week of “Introduction to Mathematical Reasoning” starts with logic. The professor writes a statement on the board: “If it's raining, the street is wet.” That's an implication: B follows from A.

“Is the converse true as well?” he asks. No! The street can also be wet because a street-cleaning truck has driven by. An equivalence only holds if both directions are true: A if and only if B.

Then he shows the truth table. An implication is only false if A is true and B is false. Finally it's about quantifiers. The negation of “For all students: they love maths” isn't “Nobody loves maths” but “There is at least one who doesn't love maths”. Many students make mistakes here.

gloss.genau: exactly (genau dann, wenn — if and only if)

questions: What statement does the professor write on the board?
When is an implication false?
What is the negation of “for all … holds”?

mathe-a22-06-logik:1.text:
In the exercise class Sophie gets a problem about sets. A is the set of students in Analysis, B the set of students in Linear Algebra. Sophie is an element of A and of B as well.

The union of A and B contains everyone who attends at least one of the two lectures. The intersection contains only the students who attend both lectures, so Sophie too.

C is the set of students who have already finished and don't attend any lectures any more. The intersection of A and C is empty, so A and C are disjoint. Finally the tutor asks: “Is A a subset of B?” Sophie thinks about it: “No, David is in Analysis but not in Linear Algebra. He's in the complement of B.”
questions: Which set contains the students who attend both lectures?
Why are A and C disjoint?
Why isn't A a subset of B?

translate.tr: Sophie is an element of A.
wrong: Sophie is a subset of A.

translate.tr: A isn't a subset of B.
wrong: A is a subset of B.
B isn't a subset of A.

mathe-a22-07-beweise:0.text:
Today the students learn two kinds of proof. First a direct proof. The hypothesis is: n is even. The claim is: n squared is even too. You write n as two times k and check it by direct calculation.

Then comes a famous proof by contradiction. The claim: the square root of two isn't rational. “We assume the opposite,” says the professor. So the assumption is: the square root of two is a fraction p over q in lowest terms.

After a few steps it follows that p is even and q is even too. But then the fraction wouldn't be in lowest terms. That's a contradiction! So the assumption was false, and the claim is proved. Sophie writes underneath: “q.e.d.” — which was to be shown.

gloss.zu: (was zu zeigen war) which was to be shown

questions: What is the hypothesis in the direct proof?
What does the professor assume?
Why is the assumption false?

mathe-a22-07-beweise:1.text:
In the exercise class Sophie has to show that for all n the sum from one to n is n times n plus one, divided by two. The tutor says: “We'll do that by induction.”

The base case is easy: for n equals one the formula is correct. In the inductive step you assume that the formula holds for n and show it for n plus one. After that the formula holds in general, for every n.

Then comes a trap. The problem claims: “n squared plus n plus 41 is always a prime number.” For n equals one, two, three that's true. But for n equals 40 the number is 41 times 41, so it isn't prime. A single counterexample disproves the statement. For the last problem Sophie needs a lemma and a case analysis: n even or n odd.
questions: How does Sophie prove the sum formula?
For which n is n squared plus n plus 41 not prime?
What disproves the statement?

wrong: The base case is very hard.

translate.tr: The formula holds for all n.
wrong: The formula doesn't hold for all n.
The formula only holds for n = 1.

mathe-a22-08-stochastik:0.text:
In the probability and statistics lecture everything starts with a dice. The random variable X is the number rolled. Each number has the same probability, so the distribution is uniform. The expected value is one plus two up to plus six, divided by six, so 3.5. Of course you can never roll a 3.5, but that's what comes out on average.

Then the professor tosses a coin ten times. The number of heads is binomially distributed, and the expected value is five. The variance measures the spread around this value. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, here about 1.6.

“If we toss the coin a thousand times,” she says, “the distribution looks almost like a normal distribution: a beautiful bell curve.”

gloss.gar: at all (gar nicht — not at all)

questions: What is the expected value for the dice?
How is the number of heads distributed for the coin?
What does the variance measure?

translate.tr: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
wrong: The variance is the square root of the standard deviation.
The standard deviation is the square of the variance.

mathe-a22-08-stochastik:1.text:
David has found an old coin. He tosses it a hundred times and gets heads 62 times. Is the coin fair? Sophie sets up a hypothesis. The null hypothesis is: the coin is fair; the probability of heads is exactly a half.

The significance level is five per cent. If the coin is fair, such an extreme result is only possible with a probability of about two per cent. That's less than five per cent, so the result is significant. They reject the null hypothesis.

The confidence interval for the probability also goes from about 0.53 to 0.72. The number 0.5 isn't in it. Even so, an error is possible: maybe David was just lucky. “It's like a conditional probability,” says Sophie, “we're never certain.”
questions: How often does David get heads?
What is the null hypothesis?
Why is an error still possible?

wrong: They set up the null hypothesis.
There will definitely be an error.

mathe-a22-09-diskrete-mathematik:0.text:
The first Discrete Mathematics class starts with a simple question: in how many ways can five friends sit in a row? For the first seat there are five possibilities, for the second four, and so on. That makes five times four times three times two times one, so five factorial: 120 arrangements. Each of them is a permutation.

Then it's about the Austrian lottery “6 out of 45”. You choose six numbers out of 45. Here the order doesn't matter. The number of possibilities is the binomial coefficient 45 choose 6: over eight million!

“Combinatorics is useful,” says the professor. “Anyone who understands it will never play the lottery again.” The students laugh.

gloss.auf: in (auf wie viele Arten — in how many ways)
gloss.weiter: on (und so weiter — and so on)
gloss.rolle: role (keine Rolle spielen — not to matter)

questions: How many arrangements are there for five friends?
What doesn't matter in the lottery?
How many possibilities are there in the lottery?

translate.tr: Five factorial is a hundred and twenty.
wrong: Five squared is a hundred and twenty.
Six factorial is a hundred and twenty.

mathe-a22-09-diskrete-mathematik:1.text:
David asks in the exercise class: “What do we need prime numbers for?” The tutor answers: “Without them there's no secure encryption on the internet.”

First they practise prime factorisation: 84 is divisible by two, then by two again, then by three and by seven. So 84 equals two times two times three times seven. Then they look for the greatest common divisor of 84 and 30. With the Euclidean algorithm it's quick: 84 divided by 30 is 2, remainder 24. Then 30 by 24, remainder 6. Then 24 by 6, remainder 0. So the GCD is 6. The algorithm keeps calling itself; that's recursion.

Finally it's about modulo. Seventeen is congruent to two modulo five, because both leave a remainder of two when divided by five. They're in the same residue class.
questions: What do you need prime numbers for?
What is the GCD of 84 and 30?
Why is seventeen congruent to two modulo five?

translate.tr: They're in the same residue class.

mathe-a22-10-pruefungen:0.text:
The winter semester is almost over. The first exam date for Analysis is at the end of January. Sophie registers for the exam online. Analysis is an important course and brings a lot of ECTS credits. A whole semester has about thirty.

Sophie and David start a study group with two other students. They meet in the library every day. The past papers help most: the problems are often similar to those in the real exam.

David has bad exam anxiety. The night before the exam he hardly sleeps. Sophie says: “You've practised so much. Breathe calmly and read every problem carefully.”
questions: When is the first exam date?
Where does the study group meet?
What helps most?

wrong: They meet in the lecture hall.
David isn't afraid of the exam at all.

mathe-a22-10-pruefungen:1.text:
Three weeks later the results come out. Sophie has passed. David is two points short; he has failed. At first he wants to drop out. “That was only your first attempt,” says Sophie. “Go to the exam review!”

At the exam review David looks at his paper. Problem three was given zero points, but the approach was correct. He goes to the professor's office hours and asks about it. The professor reads the problem again: “You're right, the approach is good. That's worth three points.”

Now David has passed. He's very relieved, because according to the curriculum Analysis is a compulsory subject. Without this exam he can't attend some courses in the summer semester.

gloss.später: later (drei Wochen später — three weeks later)

questions: How many points is David short?
Which problem was given zero points?
Why is David so relieved?

translate.tr: That was only your first attempt.
wrong: That was already your last attempt.
That was your first exam ever.

pflege-a11-01-erster-tag:0.text:
Olena is new at the hospital. She is a nurse. Today is her first day on ward three.

A woman comes and says: “Good morning! My name is Mrs Becker. I'm the ward manager.” Olena says: “Good morning! My name is Olena Kovalenko.”

Mrs Becker shows Olena the ward. There are twelve rooms here. A patient is in room five. His name is Mr Schmidt. Then a doctor comes. His name is Doctor Wagner. He says: “Welcome!”
questions: Who is new at the hospital?
How many rooms are on the ward?
Who is in room five?

translate.tr: The patient is in room five.
wrong: The patient is in room three.
The doctor is standing in room five.
The female patient is in room five.

translate.tr: Olena is new on the ward.
wrong: Olena has worked on the ward for a long time.

pflege-a11-01-erster-tag:1.text:
The early shift starts at six o'clock. Today Olena is working with Tom. Tom is her colleague. He is very nice.

Olena and Tom go to room five. Olena asks: “Good morning, Mr Schmidt! How are you feeling?” Mr Schmidt says: “Fine, thanks. But the bed isn't comfortable.”

Tom helps Olena. They make the bed together. Then Mr Schmidt reads Olena's name badge. He says: “Olena — a beautiful name!”

gloss.machen: make; (das Bett machen) to make the bed
gloss.name: name

questions: When does the early shift start?
Who is Tom?
What isn't good?

translate.tr: How are you feeling, Mr Schmidt?
wrong: What is your name, Mr Schmidt?
Where do you work, Mr Schmidt?

translate.tr: Tom helps Olena with the bed.
wrong: Olena helps Tom with the bed.
Tom helps Olena with the room.
Tom makes the bed without Olena.

pflege-a11-02-koerper:0.text:
Olena goes to room seven. Mrs Wolf is lying there. She is eighty years old. Olena shakes her hand and asks: “Good morning, Mrs Wolf! How are you feeling?”

Mrs Wolf says: “Not good. My head hurts. And my stomach too.” Olena asks: “And your back?” — “No, my back is fine.”

Olena says: “Please open your eyes. Please raise your arm. Good! And now your leg.” Then Olena calls the doctor.

gloss.gibt: gives; (die Hand geben) to shake hands

questions: How old is Mrs Wolf?
What hurts Mrs Wolf?
Whom does Olena call?

pflege-a11-02-koerper:1.text:
Doctor Wagner comes to room seven. He says: “Mrs Wolf, please open your mouth.” He looks at her teeth and throat. The throat is red.

Mrs Wolf says: “My knee hurts too.” The doctor says: “Please show me your knee.” The knee is swollen. Her chest and fingers are fine.

At the end Mrs Wolf says: “I can't hear well in my left ear.” Doctor Wagner writes everything down.
questions: What is the throat like?
What is swollen?
In which ear does Mrs Wolf hear badly?

pflege-a11-03-uhrzeit:0.text:
It's six o'clock. The early shift begins. Olena is on time, but Tom is late. He comes at quarter past six. “Sorry!” he says.

At half past six they make the beds. At seven o'clock there is breakfast. Mrs Wolf asks: “What time is it?” Olena says: “It's quarter to eight.”

At nine o'clock there is a break. It lasts half an hour. Olena drinks a coffee. After ten minutes Mrs Becker calls: “Olena, please come here!”

gloss.halbe: half; (eine halbe Stunde) half an hour
gloss.machen: make; (die Betten machen) to make the beds
gloss.vor: before; (Viertel vor acht) quarter to eight
gloss.nach: after; (Viertel nach) quarter past; (nach zehn Minuten) after ten minutes

questions: When does Tom come?
When is breakfast?
How long is the break?

translate.tr: The break lasts half an hour.
wrong: The shift lasts half an hour.

pflege-a11-03-uhrzeit:1.text:
At ten o'clock Olena takes Mrs Wolf's temperature. She has thirty-eight degrees. That's a fever!

Olena goes to the phone and calls Doctor Wagner. He says: “I'll come in twenty minutes.”

Then the phone rings. It's Mrs Wolf's daughter. She asks: “Does my mother have an appointment today?” Olena says: “Yes, at two p.m. Your number, please?” The daughter says the number, and Olena writes it down.
questions: What temperature does Mrs Wolf have?
Whom does Olena call?
When is the appointment?

wrong: Mrs Wolf has a normal temperature.
I'm calling the doctor into the room.

translate.tr: The appointment is at two p.m.
wrong: The appointment is at four o'clock.
The break is at two p.m.

pflege-a11-04-dienstplan:0.text:
The new rota hangs in the office. Olena reads it. On Monday and Tuesday she is on the early shift. On Wednesday she is off.

On Thursday and Friday she is on the late shift. And at the weekend? Then she is on night shift.

Tom says: “Today is Monday. This week we work together a lot!” Olena laughs: “Yes, but at the weekend I work alone.”
questions: When is Olena off?
What does Olena have at the weekend?
Where does the rota hang?

translate.tr: Today I'm on the late shift.
wrong: Tomorrow I'm on the late shift.
Today I'm on the night shift.

pflege-a11-04-dienstplan:1.text:
It's twelve o'clock. Olena and Tom are taking a break. Tom is tired. He says: “I'm on the early shift tomorrow. But my son is ill.”

He asks: “Olena, can we swap? You work tomorrow morning and I work at the weekend.” Olena says: “Yes, sure!”

Mrs Becker changes the rota. Tomorrow Olena's shift starts at six o'clock. At two p.m. she finishes work. In August she is on holiday.
questions: Who is ill?
When does Olena finish work tomorrow?
When is Olena on holiday?

translate.tr: I finish work at two p.m.
wrong: I start work at two p.m.
I finish work at four o'clock.

pflege-a11-05-befinden:0.text:
In the morning Olena comes to Mr Schmidt. She asks: “Did you sleep well?” Mr Schmidt says: “No, I slept badly. My back hurts.”

Mrs Wolf is ill too. She is sad and afraid. She asks: “Will I be healthy again soon?” Olena says: “Yes, Mrs Wolf. Today you're already better.”

Mrs Wolf smiles. “Thank you, Olena. You're very kind.”
questions: How did Mr Schmidt sleep?
Where is Mr Schmidt in pain?
Who is afraid?

pflege-a11-05-befinden:1.text:
At night Mrs Wolf presses the call button. Olena is on night shift and comes at once. “Do you need help?” she asks.

Mrs Wolf says: “I feel dizzy. And I'm so cold.” Olena brings a blanket. Then she takes her temperature. It is normal.

Olena says: “Breathe very calmly. Do you feel sick too?” — “No,” says Mrs Wolf. After ten minutes she is warm. Olena shows her the call button again: “Ring if you need help.”

gloss.brauchen: to need; (Brauchen Sie …?) Do you need …?

questions: What does Olena bring?
What is the temperature like?
Does Mrs Wolf feel sick?

wrong: Olena takes away a warm blanket.

pflege-a11-06-essen:0.text:
At seven o'clock Olena brings breakfast. There is bread, cheese and jam. Mr Schmidt is hungry. He eats two slices of bread.

Olena asks: “What would you like to drink? Tea or coffee?” Mr Schmidt says: “Tea, please. And a glass of water.”

Mrs Wolf doesn't eat much. She doesn't drink much either. Olena says: “Mrs Wolf, please drink more water. It's important.” There is soup for lunch. Dinner is at six p.m.
questions: What does Mr Schmidt drink?
Who drinks too little?
When is dinner?

translate.tr: What would you like to drink?
wrong: What would you like to eat?

pflege-a11-06-essen:1.text:
For lunch Tom brings the trays. He puts a tray on Mrs Wolf's table. There is soup and bread.

Tom asks: “Do you like it?” Mrs Wolf says: “The soup tastes good. But it's too hot.” After ten minutes she eats the soup. Then she says: “I'm full.”

In the afternoon Mrs Wolf is thirsty. Tom brings a cup of tea. The glass of water is empty. He brings fresh water too.
questions: What is the soup like?
What does Tom bring in the afternoon?
What is the glass like?

pflege-a11-07-pflegewagen:0.text:
Olena gets the care trolley ready. On the trolley there are gloves, masks and plasters. The medicines are in a box.

At eight o'clock Olena goes to Mr Schmidt. She puts on gloves. Mr Schmidt gets two tablets and an injection. He asks: “What kind of medicine is that?” Olena says: “For the pain.”

Then she brings the scales. Mr Schmidt weighs eighty kilos.

gloss.für: for; (was für ein) what kind of

questions: Where are the medicines?
What does Mr Schmidt get?
How much does Mr Schmidt weigh?

pflege-a11-07-pflegewagen:1.text:
Mrs Wolf wants to take a shower. Olena says to Tom: “I need help. Can you get the wheelchair, please?” Tom gets the wheelchair.

In the bathroom the soap has run out. Olena asks: “Tom, can you bring soap and two towels, please?” Tom brings everything.

After the shower Mrs Wolf has a plaster on her arm. Olena needs scissors. Then she gives Mrs Wolf the tablets in a cup.

gloss.zu: to; (sagt zu Tom) says to Tom

questions: What does Mrs Wolf want?
Who gets the wheelchair?
Where are the tablets?

wrong: Can you take the wheelchair away?

pflege-a11-08-koerperpflege:0.text:
In the morning Olena helps Mr Schmidt wash. Mr Schmidt can't walk well. Olena asks: “Would you like to take a shower today?” Mr Schmidt says: “No, not today. I'll wash at the sink.”

Olena brings a clean towel and the toothbrush. Then Mr Schmidt combs his hair. The comb is old, but good.

Later Mr Schmidt says: “I need to go to the toilet.” Olena helps him. The towel is dirty now. She brings a new one.

gloss.muss: must; (ich muss auf die Toilette) I need the toilet

questions: Where does Mr Schmidt wash?
What is the comb like?
What is dirty at the end?

translate.tr: Would you like to take a shower today?
wrong: Would you like to wash today?
Would you like to take a shower tomorrow?

translate.tr: I need to go to the toilet.
wrong: I need to go to the bathroom.
He needs to go to the toilet.

pflege-a11-08-koerperpflege:1.text:
Mrs Wolf doesn't want to stay in bed today. She wants to get dressed. Olena opens the wardrobe. Her clothes are there.

First Mrs Wolf takes off her nightgown. Then she puts on a shirt and trousers. The trousers are a bit big. Her feet are cold. Olena brings warm socks.

At the end Olena asks: “Where are your shoes?” Mrs Wolf laughs: “Under the bed!”

gloss.zieht: pulls; (zieht … an / aus) puts on / takes off

questions: What does Mrs Wolf take off first?
What are the trousers like?
Where are the shoes?

translate.tr: Mrs Wolf takes off her nightgown.
wrong: Mrs Wolf puts on her nightgown.
Mrs Wolf takes off her trousers.

pflege-a11-09-familie:0.text:
On Sunday Mrs Wolf's family comes. Her son Peter is here. He lives in Munich. His wife and the two grandchildren come too.

Peter asks Olena: “How is my mother?” Olena says: “She's better today. She doesn't have a fever any more.”

Mrs Wolf also has a daughter. Her name is Anna and she lives in Hamburg. She calls in the evening. Mr Wolf, Mrs Wolf's husband, has already died. So Peter's father is no longer alive.
questions: Where does Peter live?
How many grandchildren come?
Who calls in the evening?

pflege-a11-09-familie:1.text:
Visiting hours are from two to seven p.m. At one p.m. a woman comes with flowers. She asks: “Can I visit Mr Schmidt? I'm his wife.”

Olena says: “The doctor is with your husband right now. Please wait here.” After ten minutes Olena says: “You can go in now. Mr Schmidt, you have a visitor!”

Mr Schmidt is very happy. His wife also has a present: a book. Relatives are very important for patients.

gloss.rein: in; (Sie können rein) you can go in

questions: When are visiting hours?
Who is the woman with the flowers?
What is the present?

translate.tr: Mr Schmidt, you have a visitor!
wrong: Mr Schmidt, there's a call for you!
Mr Schmidt, you have a present!

pflege-a11-10-im-zimmer:0.text:
It's warm in the room. Mr Schmidt says: “Olena, could you open the window, please?” Olena opens the window. Now the air is fresh.

Then Doctor Wagner comes. He sits down on the chair next to the bed. Olena closes the door. The doctor says: “Mr Schmidt, tomorrow you can go home.”

Mr Schmidt is happy. In the evening he packs his things. The clothes are in the wardrobe, the books are on the table. At ten p.m. Olena switches off the light.
questions: What does Olena open?
When can Mr Schmidt go home?
Where are the books?

translate.tr: Could you open the window, please?
wrong: Could you close the window, please?
Could you open the door, please?

translate.tr: The clothes are in the wardrobe.
wrong: The clothes are on the chair.
The bag is in the wardrobe.

pflege-a11-10-im-zimmer:1.text:
At night it isn't quiet on ward three. In room four the TV is very loud. Mrs Wolf presses the call button. She says: “The TV is bothering me. I can't sleep.”

Olena goes to room four. A man is sitting in bed there. He is looking for his glasses. Olena finds the glasses in his bag. Then she says: “Please turn the TV down.”

After that she brings Mrs Wolf a new pillow. Mrs Wolf puts her phone on the table and finally falls asleep.
questions: What is loud in room four?
Where does Olena find the glasses?
What does Olena bring Mrs Wolf?

pflege-a12-01-schmerzen:0.text:
Mr Yilmaz has been on ward three since yesterday. He is fifty-five years old and has stomach problems. In the morning he presses the call button. Olena comes at once.

“I'm in pain,” says Mr Yilmaz. Olena asks: “How long have you had the pain?” — “For an hour. It came very suddenly.”

“On a scale from zero to ten: how bad is the pain?” Mr Yilmaz thinks for a moment. “Seven. It's stabbing and burning.” Olena writes everything down. Yesterday the pain was only mild. Today it is severe.

gloss.tagen: days; (in drei Tagen) in three days

questions: How long has Mr Yilmaz been on ward three?
Which number does Mr Yilmaz say?
What was the pain like yesterday?

translate.tr: How long have you had the pain?
wrong: How long will the pain last?
The pain went away very suddenly.

pflege-a12-01-schmerzen:1.text:
Olena keeps asking: “Where exactly does it hurt? Please show me the spot.” Mr Yilmaz points to his stomach. “Here. And I have a headache too.”

Olena presses carefully on his stomach. “Does it hurt when I press here?” — “Yes, a lot!” Then Mr Yilmaz says: “I can't bear the pain any more.”

Olena calls Doctor Wagner. He says: “Mr Yilmaz will get a painkiller.” Olena also brings a hot-water bottle for the stomach ache. After half an hour Mr Yilmaz can move his legs again and sleeps a little.

gloss.gegen: towards (n gegen unendlich — n tends to infinity)
gloss.halben: half (ein halbes Jahr — half a year)

questions: Where does Mr Yilmaz have pain?
Whom does Olena call?
What does Olena bring for the stomach ache?

wrong: Please tell me where the spot is.

translate.tr: Does it hurt when I press here?
wrong: Does it hurt when you press here?
Does it hurt when I touch here?
Mr Yilmaz doesn't want a painkiller.
Mr Yilmaz gets a hot-water bottle.

pflege-a12-02-mobilisation:0.text:
Mrs Wolf fell last night. She wanted to go to the toilet on her own. Luckily she only has a bruise on her arm.

Today Olena helps her get up. “First sit on the edge of the bed,” she says. “And now stand up very slowly. I'll support you.”

Mrs Wolf is standing. She feels a bit dizzy. Olena waits. Then she brings the rollator. “With the rollator it's safe,” she says. “But please be careful and don't get up alone at night. Ring the bell!”

gloss.zum: zum Beispiel — for example; zum Glück — luckily
gloss.am: at, on (am Anfang — at the beginning)
gloss.aufstehen: to get up; (beim Aufstehen) getting up

questions: When did Mrs Wolf fall?
Where does Mrs Wolf have a bruise?
What does Olena bring?

translate.tr: I'll support you by the arm.
wrong: You'll support me by the arm.

translate.tr: Please don't get up on your own.
wrong: Please get up on your own.
Please don't walk on your own.

pflege-a12-02-mobilisation:1.text:
Mr Schmidt already walks well. Today he wants to walk to the window at the end of the corridor. Tom goes with him. “Hold on tight to the rollator,” Tom says.

Step by step they walk along the corridor. After twenty steps Mr Schmidt takes a break. “My balance isn't so good,” he says.

There are stairs by the window. Mr Schmidt asks: “Can we take the stairs?” Tom laughs: “No, not today. We'll take the lift to the cafeteria. They have cake there.”

gloss.zum: zum Beispiel — for example; zum Glück — luckily

questions: Where does Mr Schmidt want to walk to?
After how many steps does he take a break?
How do they get to the cafeteria?

pflege-a12-03-grundpflege:0.text:
Mr Yilmaz can't take a shower today. Olena washes him in bed. Afterwards she sees that the skin on his legs is very dry. “I'll put cream on your legs,” she says. “This cream is good for dry skin.”

Mr Yilmaz asks: “Can I shave too?” — “Of course. Where is your shaver?” — “In the wardrobe, in the grey bag.”

Olena gets the shaver and a mirror. Mr Yilmaz shaves himself. Then he combs his hair. “Now I feel like a new man,” he says.
questions: Where is the skin very dry?
Where is the shaver?
What does Mr Yilmaz do on his own?

translate.tr: I'll put cream on your legs.
wrong: I'll put cream on your arms.
Would you like to comb your hair?

pflege-a12-03-grundpflege:1.text:
Mrs Wolf sweated in the night. Her nightgown and the bed linen are wet. Olena and Tom change the bed.

First Olena fills a basin with warm water. She washes Mrs Wolf with the washcloth and dries her well. “Please turn on your side,” says Tom. Mrs Wolf turns over. Tom takes away the old linen and puts on the new.

Finally Olena cleans Mrs Wolf's denture. She puts it in a cup of water. Mrs Wolf smiles: “Thank you! Now everything is fresh.”

gloss.zum: zum Beispiel — for example; zum Glück — luckily

questions: Why is the bed linen wet?
What does Olena wash Mrs Wolf with?
Where is the denture at the end?

translate.tr: We're changing the bed linen now.
wrong: We're washing the bed linen now.
We'll change the bed linen tomorrow.
Please sit on the edge of the bed.

translate.tr: The basin is full of water.
wrong: The glass is full of water.

pflege-a12-04-essen-reichen:0.text:
Mr Becker had a stroke. His right hand is weak, and he can't swallow well. That's why he only gets soft food.

Today there is fish with mashed potatoes. Olena sits down next to him. She puts a napkin down for him and cuts the fish into very small pieces. “Would you like to try on your own?” she asks. Mr Becker takes the spoon in his left hand.

It's slow, but it works. He doesn't need the fork and the knife. After twenty minutes the plate is empty. Olena is proud of him.

gloss.stolz: proud (stolz auf sich — proud of herself)

questions: What is there today?
Which hand is weak?
How long does Mr Becker eat?

translate.tr: Shall I cut the fish into small pieces?
wrong: Shall I cut the meat into small pieces?
Will you cut the fish into small pieces?

translate.tr: He takes the spoon in his left hand.
wrong: He takes the fork in his left hand.
He takes the spoon in his right hand.

pflege-a12-04-essen-reichen:1.text:
In the afternoon Tom comes with the menu. The patients can order tomorrow's food. There are three menus.

Mr Yilmaz has diabetes. He mustn't eat much sugar. Tom says: “Menu two is good for you. And to drink? Juice has a lot of sugar. Better tea or water.”

Mrs Wolf has a nut allergy. She orders menu one. She'd like just a small portion. For breakfast she orders yoghurt and a coffee with milk.

gloss.zum: zum Beispiel — for example; zum Glück — luckily
gloss.gegen: towards (n gegen unendlich — n tends to infinity)

questions: Who has diabetes?
What is Mrs Wolf allergic to?
What does Mrs Wolf order for breakfast?

translate.tr: Juice has a lot of sugar.
wrong: Tea has a lot of sugar.

translate.tr: I'd like just a small portion.

pflege-a12-05-vitalzeichen:0.text:
Every morning Olena measures the vital signs. First she goes to Mr Yilmaz. She puts the cuff around his arm. His blood pressure is one hundred and sixty over one hundred. “That's too high,” says Olena.

Then she takes his pulse. It's eighty-six, that's normal. Because Mr Yilmaz has diabetes, she checks his blood sugar too. The value is low. Olena gives him a glass of juice.

She records all the values. Then she calls Doctor Wagner and tells him: “Mr Yilmaz's blood pressure is too high.”

gloss.alle: every (alle zwanzig Minuten — every twenty minutes)

questions: What is Mr Yilmaz's blood pressure like?
What does Olena give him?
Whom does Olena call?

translate.tr: The blood pressure is too high.
wrong: The blood pressure is too low.

translate.tr: I'm going to take your pulse now.
wrong: I'm going to take your blood pressure now.
You're going to take my pulse now.
Olena records only the blood pressure.

pflege-a12-05-vitalzeichen:1.text:
Since yesterday Mrs Wolf has had problems with her breathing. She is getting oxygen. Olena regularly checks how she is breathing. “Please breathe in deeply … and out again.”

Then Olena takes her temperature with the thermometer: 37.8 degrees. That's a bit high. After that she weighs Mrs Wolf. Her weight has been the same for three days: sixty kilos.

Olena writes everything in the chart. On the ward round Doctor Wagner reads the chart and says: “Good. We'll keep measuring every day.”

gloss.tagen: days; (in drei Tagen) in three days
gloss.hoch: up; (here) part of hochladen — to upload

questions: What is Mrs Wolf getting?
How much does Mrs Wolf weigh?
Where does Olena write everything?

translate.tr: The weight has been the same for three days.
wrong: The weight has gone up in three days.
The temperature has been the same for three days.

translate.tr: We take the blood pressure regularly.
wrong: We rarely take the blood pressure.
We check the blood sugar regularly.

pflege-a12-06-medikamente:0.text:
Mr Schmidt can go home tomorrow. Olena explains his medicines to him. “You take this small tablet in the morning, before breakfast. You need to have an empty stomach for it.”

“And the big one?” asks Mr Schmidt. “You take that in the evening, after eating.” Then Olena shows him the drops: “Ten drops in a glass of water, three times a day.”

For his knee he gets an ointment. “Here's the doctor's prescription too,” says Olena. “You'll get the medicines at the pharmacy.”

gloss.hause: home (nach Hause — home; zu Hause — at home)

questions: When does Mr Schmidt take the small tablet?
How often does he take the drops?
Where will he get the medicines?

translate.tr: You take this tablet in the morning.
wrong: You take this tablet in the evening.
You take these drops in the morning.

translate.tr: You need a prescription for the ointment.
wrong: You don't need a prescription for the ointment.
You need a prescription for the drops.

pflege-a12-06-medikamente:1.text:
Since yesterday Mr Yilmaz has been getting a new medicine. Doctor Wagner prescribed it. Today Mr Yilmaz is very tired and feels sick.

Olena reads the package leaflet. It says: tiredness and nausea are side effects. She tells the doctor. Doctor Wagner says: “We'll give the medicine as an infusion now. That way it works better.”

In the evening Mr Yilmaz asks: “Do I still have to take the capsule? I forgot it this morning.” Olena looks at the chart and says: “No, the pack is empty. It's in the infusion now.”
questions: Who prescribed the medicine?
What are the side effects?
How does Mr Yilmaz get the medicine now?

translate.tr: The doctor prescribes a new medicine.
wrong: The nurse prescribes a new medicine.

pflege-a12-07-notfall:0.text:
It's three o'clock at night. Olena hears a loud noise from room eight. She runs there at once. Mr Becker is lying on the bathroom floor. He has fallen.

“Mr Becker! Can you hear me?” He doesn't answer. He is unconscious, but he is breathing. Olena presses the alarm. “Emergency in room eight!” she calls.

After a minute Tom comes. “What happened?” — “He fell and he's unconscious. Call the doctor on duty, quick!” Tom phones. Two minutes later Doctor Wagner is there.

gloss.später: later (eine Stunde später — an hour later)

questions: Where is Mr Becker lying?
What does Olena do first?
Whom does Tom call?

translate.tr: Call the doctor on duty, quick!

pflege-a12-07-notfall:1.text:
Doctor Wagner examines Mr Becker. There is a wound on his head. It is bleeding heavily. “Is it dangerous?” asks Olena. “No, the wound isn't deep,” says the doctor. “But he needs a dressing.”

Tom puts on a dressing. After five minutes Mr Becker opens his eyes. “Where am I?” he asks. Olena says: “In hospital. You fell. Stay completely calm.”

Doctor Wagner wants to examine his head more closely. An ambulance takes Mr Becker to another hospital for an examination. There is still blood on the bathroom floor. Tom cleans it up.

gloss.am: at, on (am Anfang — at the beginning)

questions: Where is the wound?
Who puts on the dressing?
What is the wound like?

pflege-a12-08-aufnahme:0.text:
A new patient comes to ward three. Olena does the admission. “Good afternoon! What's your name, please?” — “My name is Dariusz Nowak.” — “Could you spell your surname, please?” — “N-O-W-A-K.”

Then Olena asks for his date of birth and address. Mr Nowak was born on the twelfth of March nineteen sixty. He lives at Gartenstraße 4.

“Do you have your health insurance card with you?” Mr Nowak gives her the card. His health insurance fund is the AOK. His emergency contact is his daughter.
questions: What is the new patient's name?
Where does Mr Nowak live?
Who is his emergency contact?

translate.tr: Do you have your health insurance card with you?
wrong: Do you have your passport with you?

pflege-a12-08-aufnahme:1.text:
Now Olena fills in the form with Mr Nowak. “What's the reason for your stay in hospital?” — “I've had heart problems for weeks.”

Olena measures his height: one metre seventy-eight. Then she asks: “What's your GP's name?” — “Doctor Krüger on Hauptstraße.”

At the end Olena says: “Please sign here at the bottom. Your signature is still missing here.” Mr Nowak signs. “And one more thing: do you have any valuables with you? Money or jewellery? We can put them in the safe.” Mr Nowak gives her his watch and his wallet.

gloss.oder: or; (at the end of a question) isn't it?

questions: What's the reason for the stay?
How tall is Mr Nowak?
What does Mr Nowak give Olena?

translate.tr: I'll fill in the form with you.
wrong: You'll fill in the form yourself.

translate.tr: Do you have any valuables with you?
wrong: Do you have any medicines with you?
Do you have any documents with you?

pflege-a12-09-ausscheidung:0.text:
Mrs Wolf rings at night. “I need the toilet,” she says quietly. She can't go to the bathroom on her own yet. Olena brings the commode to the bed and helps her.

Afterwards Olena asks: “Have you had a bowel movement today?” Mrs Wolf blushes. “That's embarrassing.” Olena says: “There's no need to be embarrassed. It's completely normal for us.”

Mrs Wolf says: “No, not for two days.” Olena writes it in the chart. Tomorrow morning she'll rinse the commode and change the pad.

gloss.mal: time (zum ersten Mal — for the first time)
gloss.ins: into the (ins Formular — in the form)
gloss.tagen: days; (in drei Tagen) in three days

questions: What does Olena bring to the bed?
Why does Mrs Wolf blush?
How long has Mrs Wolf not had a bowel movement?

translate.tr: I need to go to the toilet.
wrong: I need to go to the bathroom.

translate.tr: There's no need to be embarrassed.
wrong: I don't need to be embarrassed.

pflege-a12-09-ausscheidung:1.text:
After the operation Mr Nowak has a catheter. The urine runs into a bag on the bed. In the morning the bag is full. Tom empties it and measures the amount: eight hundred millilitres.

“The urine is very dark and smells strong,” Tom says to Olena. “Mr Nowak is drinking too little.” Olena brings Mr Nowak a big bottle of water.

In the room next door Mrs Wolf now has diarrhoea. Before she was constipated, now it's the other way round. Olena tells Doctor Wagner on the ward round.

gloss.am: at, on (am Anfang — at the beginning)

questions: How much urine is in the bag?
What is the urine like?
What does Olena bring Mr Nowak?

translate.tr: She has had diarrhoea since yesterday.
wrong: She has been constipated since yesterday.
He has had diarrhoea since yesterday.

pflege-a12-10-uebergabe:0.text:
The night shift ends at six o'clock. Olena does the handover for her colleague Sabine. Sabine takes notes.

“Room five: Mr Nowak is stable. Nothing unusual,” Olena reports. “Room seven: Mrs Wolf was restless in the night. She slept little. Please take her blood pressure at lunchtime today. That's important.”

“And Mr Schmidt?” asks Sabine. “He's being discharged today. His wife is picking him up at ten o'clock.”
questions: When does the night shift end?
What was Mrs Wolf like in the night?
Who is picking up Mr Schmidt?

translate.tr: Mrs Wolf was restless in the night.
wrong: Mrs Wolf slept well in the night.
Mrs Wolf was restless during the day.

translate.tr: Mr Schmidt is being discharged today.
wrong: Mr Schmidt is being admitted today.
Mr Schmidt is being discharged tomorrow.

pflege-a12-10-uebergabe:1.text:
Sabine asks: “What are my tasks after the ward round?” Olena gives her a note. All the tasks for the early shift are on it.

“I've already done Mr Becker's dressing,” says Olena. “But Mr Nowak's catheter bag isn't empty yet. You need to do that later.”

“Are you done?” asks Sabine. “Almost. Can you remind me of something? Tomorrow I have to go to the doctor at ten. I'm swapping shifts with Tom.” Sabine laughs: “No problem. Sleep well!”

gloss.alle: every (alle zwanzig Minuten — every twenty minutes)
gloss.zum: zum Beispiel — for example; zum Glück — luckily

questions: What does Olena give Sabine?
What has Olena already done?
When does Olena have to go to the doctor tomorrow?

wrong: I haven't done the dressing yet.
A colleague will do the dressing.

translate.tr: Can you remind me about the appointment?
wrong: Can you book me an appointment?

common.am: at the, on the (an dem); on (a day)
common.dabei: at the same time; in doing so
common.name: name
